topics.name: Complement lookup
topics.signal: While scanning, look up a needed partner (target minus x, a seen prefix) in a hash map of earlier values.

topics.name: Frequency counting
topics.signal: Count occurrences to compare multisets or find the most or least common items.

topics.name: Group by canonical key
topics.signal: Items are equal under some normalization (sorted letters, a tuple of counts), so bucket them by that key.

topics.name: Set membership
topics.signal: Existence checks in a hash set, such as starting a run only where x-1 is absent.

topics.name: Array as its own hash
topics.signal: Values lie in 1..n, so mark by sign or swap each value into its own index for O(1) space.

topics.name: Opposite ends
topics.signal: Pointers at both ends of a sorted array or string move inward by a rule (pair sum, container, palindrome).

topics.name: Fast and slow
topics.signal: Two speeds over a list or sequence: find a cycle, the middle, or the nth from the end.

topics.name: Read and write pointers
topics.signal: Compact or partition in place with a write index trailing a read index (remove duplicates, move zeroes, colors).

topics.name: k-sum
topics.signal: Sort, fix one or more values, then two pointers for the rest, skipping duplicates.

topics.name: Walk two sequences
topics.signal: Advance through two sorted sequences together: merge, intersect, or check a subsequence.

topics.name: Fixed-size window
topics.signal: The window is exactly k long; add the new element and drop the old one each step.

topics.name: Longest valid window
topics.signal: Grow right, shrink left only when the window breaks a rule; maximize its length.

topics.name: Shortest valid window
topics.signal: Once the window satisfies the rule, shrink left while it still does; minimize its length.

topics.name: Count windows
topics.signal: Count subarrays meeting a rule, often exactly(K) = atMost(K) - atMost(K-1).

topics.name: Range sums
topics.signal: Precompute prefix sums (1D or 2D) so any range total is a subtraction.

topics.name: Prefix sum with a hash map
topics.signal: Count or find subarrays with a given sum or remainder by storing earlier prefix values.

topics.name: Difference array
topics.signal: Many range updates, read once at the end: add at start, subtract after end, then prefix-sum.

topics.name: Left and right passes
topics.signal: Combine a prefix pass and a suffix pass, such as product except self or max-to-the-left arrays.

topics.name: Lower and upper bound
topics.signal: First or last position meeting a condition in a sorted array.

topics.name: Rotated array
topics.signal: A sorted array rotated at an unknown pivot; decide which half is sorted.

topics.name: Sorted matrix
topics.signal: Search a matrix whose rows and columns are sorted, as one array or from a corner.

topics.name: Search on a property
topics.signal: No sorted order, but a monotone property splits the array (peak element, bad version).

topics.name: Partition two arrays
topics.signal: Binary search a cut across two sorted arrays, as in the median of two sorted arrays or kth across them.

topics.name: Search the answer with a check
topics.signal: Minimize the maximum (or maximize the minimum): binary search the answer and test it greedily (ship in D days, Koko).

topics.name: Kth by counting
topics.signal: Binary search a value and count how many items are at most it (kth smallest in a matrix or of pair distances).

topics.name: Custom comparator
topics.signal: The answer depends on sorting by a non-obvious key or comparator (largest number, reorder logs).

topics.name: Counting and bucket sort
topics.signal: Bounded values or frequencies allow O(n) bucketing (top k by buckets, maximum gap, h-index).

topics.name: Quickselect
topics.signal: Find the kth element or partition around it without fully sorting.

topics.name: Merge intervals
topics.signal: Sort by start and merge overlaps, or insert one interval into a sorted list.

topics.name: Greedy by end
topics.signal: Sort by end time and keep the earliest finishing (non-overlapping intervals, arrows, max meetings).

topics.name: Count overlaps
topics.signal: How many intervals overlap at once (meeting rooms, car pooling): sort endpoints or use a heap.

topics.name: Bracket matching
topics.signal: Match opening and closing symbols, or track depth and validity of nesting.

topics.name: Evaluate nested expressions
topics.signal: Calculators, RPN, decode string: push context on open, combine on close.

topics.name: Stack as history
topics.signal: Later items cancel or modify earlier ones (asteroid collision, backspace, simplify path).

topics.name: Next greater or smaller
topics.signal: For each element, the next or previous element that is greater or smaller (daily temperatures).

topics.name: Spans and contributions
topics.signal: Each element's reach left and right gives areas or counts (largest rectangle, sum of subarray minimums).

topics.name: Pop to build the best sequence
topics.signal: Build the smallest or largest result by popping worse earlier choices (remove k digits, smallest subsequence).

topics.name: Reverse links
topics.signal: Reverse the whole list, a sublist, or k-groups by rewiring next pointers.

topics.name: Merge, split, reorder
topics.signal: Merge sorted lists, partition around a value, or split and interleave halves, usually with a dummy head.

topics.name: Clone or flatten
topics.signal: Deep copy with extra pointers, or flatten nested lists, using a map or interleaved copies.

topics.name: Combine children
topics.signal: A node's answer comes from its children's results (height, diameter, balanced, subtree checks).

topics.name: Pass state down
topics.signal: Carry depth, bounds or the path so far from parent to child (validate BST by range, good nodes).

topics.name: Path sums
topics.signal: Root-to-leaf or any-node paths: return one branch upward and update a global best (max path sum).

topics.name: Build or serialize
topics.signal: Construct a tree from traversals, or encode and decode one.

topics.name: Lowest common ancestor
topics.signal: Find where two nodes' paths from the root diverge.

topics.name: BST inorder order
topics.signal: Inorder traversal is sorted: kth smallest, validate, recover swapped nodes.

topics.name: Navigate a BST
topics.signal: Go left or right by comparison to search, insert, delete, or trim to a range.

topics.name: Prefix lookup
topics.signal: Insert words and query prefixes or whole words (autocomplete, replace words).

topics.name: Trie with DFS
topics.signal: Search many words at once over a board or within words (word search II, concatenated words).

topics.name: Bitwise trie
topics.signal: Store numbers bit by bit to find the maximum XOR pair.

topics.name: Top k
topics.signal: Keep the k best seen so far in a size-k heap.

topics.name: K-way merge
topics.signal: Merge k sorted lists or rows, or find the kth smallest across them.

topics.name: Two heaps
topics.signal: Keep a running median or balance with a max-heap and a min-heap.

topics.name: Schedule by heap
topics.signal: Repeatedly take the cheapest, earliest or most frequent available item (task scheduler, IPO, reorganize).

topics.name: Connected components
topics.signal: Count or label groups with DFS or BFS over an adjacency list.

topics.name: Fewest steps by BFS
topics.signal: Unweighted shortest path where each move costs one (word ladder, open the lock).

topics.name: Multi-source BFS
topics.signal: Start BFS from many sources at once and spread in levels (rotting oranges, walls and gates).

topics.name: Cycle detection
topics.signal: Detect a cycle with three-color DFS in a directed graph, or parent tracking in an undirected one.

topics.name: Two-coloring
topics.signal: Split nodes into two groups with no edge inside a group.

topics.name: BFS over states
topics.signal: A node is a whole state (position plus keys, a mask, a board), and BFS explores state changes.

topics.name: Flood fill
topics.signal: DFS or BFS over cells to mark regions (number of islands, max area).

topics.name: Start from the border
topics.signal: Search inward from edge cells to find what is or isn't reachable (surrounded regions, Pacific Atlantic).

topics.name: Union-find connectivity
topics.signal: Merge sets as edges arrive and ask if two items are connected (redundant connection, provinces).

topics.name: Union by shared key
topics.signal: Union items that share an attribute (accounts merge, similar strings, equations).

topics.name: Offline unions
topics.signal: Sort edges and queries, then union in order to answer queries (limited path lengths, Kruskal-like).

topics.name: Dijkstra
topics.signal: Nonnegative weights: pop the closest node from a heap (network delay, path with minimum effort).

topics.name: Limited edges
topics.signal: Cheapest path with at most k edges: Bellman-Ford rounds or BFS with a step count.

topics.name: All pairs
topics.signal: Distances between every pair: Floyd-Warshall on a small graph.

topics.name: Subsets
topics.signal: Include or exclude each element, skipping equal neighbors when there are duplicates.

topics.name: Permutations
topics.signal: Order matters: a used[] array or swapping, with duplicate skipping.

topics.name: Combination sum
topics.signal: Choose items to hit a target with rules on reuse, pruning when over.

topics.name: Constraint placement
topics.signal: Place items under constraints and undo on conflict (n-queens, sudoku).

topics.name: Grid path search
topics.signal: DFS on a grid marking visited and unmarking on return (word search).

topics.name: Partition a string
topics.signal: Cut a string or array into valid pieces (palindrome partitioning, IP addresses, word break II).

topics.name: Take or skip
topics.signal: dp[i] chooses between using item i or not, from the last one or two states (house robber, climbing stairs).

topics.name: Best ending here
topics.signal: Track the best subarray ending at each index (max subarray, max product).

topics.name: Increasing subsequence
topics.signal: Longest increasing or chained subsequence, O(n^2) or patience sorting with binary search.

topics.name: Count ways
topics.signal: Number of ways or decodings, summing smaller states (decode ways).

topics.name: Split points
topics.signal: dp[i] tries every last cut j < i (word break, min cuts, perfect squares).

topics.name: Reach and minimum steps
topics.signal: Fewest steps or cheapest cost to reach the end (jump game II, min cost tickets).

topics.name: Grid paths
topics.signal: Count or minimize paths moving only right or down, with obstacles or costs.

topics.name: Largest square or rectangle
topics.signal: dp of the biggest shape ending at each cell (maximal square).

topics.name: Two strings
topics.signal: dp[i][j] over prefixes of two strings (LCS, edit distance, interleaving, distinct subsequences).

topics.name: Palindromes
topics.signal: Palindromic substrings or subsequences by expanding or by interval dp.

topics.name: Pattern matching
topics.signal: Match with wildcards or regex operators like * and ?.

topics.name: 0/1 knapsack
topics.signal: Each item used at most once to reach a sum or capacity (partition equal subset, target sum).

topics.name: Unbounded knapsack
topics.signal: Items can be reused (coin change, combination sum IV).

topics.name: Node states
topics.signal: Each node returns a few states such as taken or not (house robber III, cameras).

topics.name: Rerooting
topics.signal: Answer for every node as root by reusing a first DFS (sum of distances in tree).

topics.name: Sort, then pick
topics.signal: After sorting, a simple local choice is optimal (assign cookies, boats, two city scheduling).

topics.name: Farthest reach
topics.signal: Track the farthest point reachable so far (jump game, gas station).

topics.name: Two passes
topics.signal: A left-to-right pass and a right-to-left pass, then combine (candy).

topics.name: Running balance
topics.signal: A running counter or balance decides each step (parentheses to add, lemonade change).

topics.name: Build the answer
topics.signal: Build the result piece by piece, always taking the best safe piece (reorganize string, monotone digits).

topics.name: XOR cancels
topics.signal: Pairs cancel under XOR (single number, missing number).

topics.name: Bit tests and counts
topics.signal: Count, test, set or clear bits (power of two, counting bits, reverse bits).

topics.name: Masks as subsets
topics.signal: Enumerate or represent subsets as bitmasks.

topics.name: Number theory
topics.signal: GCD, primes, divisibility, modular arithmetic.

topics.name: Digits and overflow
topics.signal: Work digit by digit, watching the 32-bit range (reverse integer, palindrome number, atoi).

topics.name: Counting formulas
topics.signal: Count with nCr, Pascal's triangle or inclusion-exclusion.

topics.name: Geometry
topics.signal: Points, lines, rectangles, areas and angles.

topics.name: Find the formula
topics.signal: Spot a pattern or closed form instead of simulating (bulb switcher, nim).

topics.name: Numbers as strings
topics.signal: Add or multiply numbers stored as strings, arrays or lists.

topics.name: KMP and Z
topics.signal: Prefix-function or Z-array for pattern search and repeated structure.

topics.name: Rolling hash
topics.signal: Rabin-Karp hashes to compare substrings fast (longest duplicate substring).

topics.name: Segment tree
topics.signal: Range queries with updates (sum, min, max), possibly lazy.

topics.name: Fenwick tree
topics.signal: Prefix sums with point updates, or counting inversions by value.

topics.name: Ordered set
topics.signal: A balanced tree or sorted container answers floor, ceiling or rank as items arrive.

topics.name: Count during merge sort
topics.signal: Count pairs across halves while merging (reverse pairs, count of smaller numbers after self).

topics.name: Split and combine
topics.signal: Solve halves recursively and combine (different ways to add parentheses, sorted array to BST).

topics.name: Caches
topics.signal: LRU or LFU: a hash map plus an ordered list for O(1) updates.

topics.name: Iterators and streams
topics.signal: Process data as it arrives or one item at a time (moving average, peeking iterator).

topics.name: Structure with fast operations
topics.signal: Support each operation in O(1) or O(log n) (min stack, randomized set, time map).

topics.name: Matrix walks
topics.signal: Spiral, rotate, transpose or diagonal traversal of a matrix.

topics.name: Apply rules step by step
topics.signal: Follow given rules exactly, tick by tick (game of life, robot moves, text justification).

topics.name: Parse and format strings
topics.signal: Parse or rebuild text by a fixed format (compress, zigzag, validate IP).

Returning a list holding one empty string for empty input instead of an empty list.

cards.q: Licence plates count as possible duplicates when one's characters can be rearranged into the other's. Bucket `n` plates into duplicate groups.
cards.a: Hash map keyed by a canonical form. Signal: items are equal under reordering, so each has a normal form such as its sorted characters. Not pairwise comparison: that is O(n^2) comparisons, while one pass with canonical keys groups everything.

cards.q: Badge numbers were issued in scattered batches. Find the longest run of consecutive numbers that all exist, in O(n) expected time.
cards.a: Hash set of values. Signal: consecutive values with no useful order, and the O(n) bound rules out ordering them first. Key step: only start counting at `x` when `x - 1` is absent, so each run is walked once.

cards.q: An unordered ledger needs auditing. Return the row numbers of two entries whose amounts add up to exactly `T`.
cards.a: Hash map from amount to row. Signal: unordered data, a pair target, and the answer must be original row numbers. Not two pointers: they need ascending order, and sorting costs O(n log n) and loses the row numbers unless you carry them along.

cards.q: Item prices are listed in ascending order and a gift card is worth exactly `T`. Find two items that use it up, with O(1) extra memory.
cards.a: Two pointers from both ends. Signal: ascending input, a pair target and an O(1) memory limit. Not a hash set: it also runs in O(n) but needs O(n) memory and ignores the given order.

cards.q: An ascending array of sensor readings contains repeats. Overwrite it so the distinct readings sit at the front, with O(1) extra memory.
cards.a: Two pointers, read and write. Signal: in-place compaction, where one index scans and the other marks the end of the kept part. Not `erase` in a loop: each call shifts the tail, so the total can reach O(n^2).

cards.q: Each minute of a video has a non-negative ad load. Find the longest stretch of consecutive minutes whose total load is at most `B`.
cards.a: Variable sliding window. Signal: a contiguous stretch, a cap, and non-negative values, so extending never lowers the total. Not prefix sums with a hashmap: those serve exact targets, and here a window gives O(n) time with O(1) memory.

cards.q: Daily profit can be positive or negative. Count the runs of consecutive days whose profit totals exactly `K`.
cards.a: Prefix sum plus hashmap. Signal: an exact target over contiguous ranges, with negatives allowed. Not sliding window: with negatives, extending can lower the total, so no rule says when to grow or shrink.

cards.q: A conveyor carries parts of many types and your bin accepts at most `K` distinct types. Find the longest consecutive section of the belt you can collect.
cards.a: Sliding window with a count map. Signal: longest contiguous section under an 'at most K' limit that stays valid when the section shrinks. Not checking all sections: that is O(n^2), while each part enters and leaves the window once.

cards.q: A chat log is a sequence of speaker ids. Find the shortest consecutive stretch in which all `M` required people speak.
cards.a: Sliding window, shrink while valid. Signal: shortest contiguous stretch that covers a required set. Key step: extend right until everyone is covered, then pull left as far as coverage holds, recording the length each time.

cards.q: A year of daily sales is final, and analysts fire a million queries for the total between two dates.
cards.a: Prefix sum. Signal: many range totals on data that never changes. Not summing per query: O(n) each is too slow, while running totals answer in O(1).

cards.q: A year of daily sales receives corrections to single days, mixed in with a million queries for the total between two dates.
cards.a: Fenwick tree or segment tree. Signal: point updates interleaved with range totals. Not prefix sums: one correction rewrites O(n) running totals, while here both operations are O(log n).

cards.q: Each of a million maintenance jobs adds load `c` to every kilometre from `l` to `r` of a highway. Only the final load of each kilometre matters.
cards.a: Difference array, a prefix sum in reverse. Signal: many range additions and a single read at the end. Not a segment tree: it works but adds a log factor, while `d[l] += c; d[r + 1] -= c` plus one running sum is O(n + q).

cards.q: A ring buffer stores distinct timestamps in ascending order, but the oldest entry sits at an unknown offset. Find it in O(log n).
cards.a: Binary search on a rotated array. Signal: ascending order with one break point, plus a log bound. Key step: compare `a[mid]` with `a[hi]` to learn which side holds the break.

cards.q: Once a build breaks, every later commit stays broken. Each test run takes ten minutes, so find the first broken commit in as few runs as possible.
cards.a: Binary search on a predicate. Signal: a yes/no property flips exactly once along an ordered sequence. Not a linear scan: it needs O(n) runs against O(log n).

cards.q: Split `n` chapters, in order, among `k` translators so the largest page load is as small as possible, with `n` up to 1e5.
cards.a: Binary search on the answer. Signal: minimise a maximum, and testing one candidate cap is a greedy O(n) scan. Not partition DP: O(k n^2) is far too slow at this size, while feasibility is monotone in the cap.

cards.q: Split `n` chapters, in order, among `k` translators to minimise the sum of the squares of their page loads, with `n` up to 500.
cards.a: Partition DP: `dp[j][i]` is the best cost for the first `i` chapters using `j` translators. Signal: the objective adds a cost over all parts, and `n` is small. Not binary search on the answer: the cost is a total over all parts, so there is no simple greedy check for a candidate value.

cards.q: Place `k` cell towers on given candidate positions along a road so that the closest pair of towers is as far apart as possible.
cards.a: Binary search on the answer. Signal: maximise a minimum, and a fixed gap `d` can be tested by placing towers greedily from the left. Not enumerating placements: the number of subsets explodes, while each check is O(n) on ordered positions.

cards.q: A forklift clears `n` pallets of boxes within `H` hours, moving at most `r` boxes per hour and working on one pallet per hour. Find the smallest `r` that meets the deadline.
cards.a: Binary search on the answer. Signal: 'smallest rate that still works', and a faster rate never hurts. Not trying every rate upward: that is O(max * n), while checking `sum(ceil(boxes / r))` at each halving step costs O(n log max).

cards.q: Daily balance changes can be negative. Find the shortest run of consecutive days with a total of at least `K`.
cards.a: Monotonic deque over prefix sums. Signal: shortest range with a lower bound on the total, and negatives allowed. Not sliding window: with negatives the total is not monotonic in length, so shrinking can skip the answer.

cards.q: You have numeric stickers like `9`, `34`, `3` and `30`. Paste them side by side to form the largest possible number.
cards.a: Custom comparator sort: put `a` before `b` when the text `a + b` beats `b + a`. Signal: the best order depends on how two items combine, not on their own values. Not numeric or plain text order: both put `30` before `3`, giving 303 where 330 is possible.

cards.q: A fixed array of 1e7 measurements sits in memory and you need its median exactly once.
cards.a: Quickselect via `nth_element`. Signal: one selection on static data, with no need for full order. Not a heap: with `k` near `n/2` it costs O(n log n) time and O(n) extra memory, while quickselect averages O(n) in place.

cards.q: Calendar entries from several people overlap. Produce a compact list of busy blocks with no overlaps.
cards.a: Merge intervals. Signal: overlapping ranges must collapse into disjoint blocks. Not pairwise overlap checks: that is O(n^2), while ordering by start lets one scan extend the current block.

cards.q: One stage, many acts with fixed start and end times. Book as many acts as possible with no overlap.
cards.a: Greedy by earliest end time. Signal: maximise the count of non-overlapping ranges. Not earliest start or shortest first: a long early act, or a short act straddling two others, breaks those rules.

cards.q: One stage, many acts with fixed start and end times, and each act pays a different fee. Book a non-overlapping set with the highest total fee.
cards.a: DP over acts ordered by end time, using binary search for the last compatible act. Signal: the ranges carry weights, so the count no longer decides. Not greedy by end time: one long, well-paid act can beat several cheap short ones.

cards.q: Workshops have fixed time ranges and each needs its own room throughout. What is the fewest rooms that fits them all?
cards.a: Sweep line over `+1` and `-1` events, or a min-heap of end times. Signal: the fewest rooms equals the peak number of simultaneous workshops. Not merging ranges: that yields busy blocks and loses how many overlap.

cards.q: Radio stations each broadcast over a time range at a fixed power. Output the moments when the strongest power on air changes.
cards.a: Sweep line with an ordered multiset of active powers. Signal: a maximum over active ranges must be known at every start and end. Not merging ranges: it drops individual powers, so you need the active set during the sweep.

cards.q: A document uses nested opening and closing tags. Check that every tag closes in the right order.
cards.a: Stack. Signal: nesting, where the most recently opened item must close first. Not counters: counts cannot catch wrong order such as ``.

cards.q: A config format nests repeat blocks, so `2{a3{b}}` expands to `abbbabbb`. Expand a given config.
cards.a: Stack of partial results, or recursion. Signal: brackets nest, so an inner block must finish before its outer block. Not a flat scan: the outer repeat count and text must be saved until the inner block closes.

cards.q: A row of people faces right. For each person, find the first taller person in front of them.
cards.a: Monotonic stack. Signal: nearest taller element for every position, with no expiry rule. Not a monotonic deque: nothing leaves by age here, so one open end is enough for O(n).

cards.q: A fixed-length block slides along a sensor stream. After each shift, report the largest reading inside the block.
cards.a: Monotonic deque. Signal: a moving-range maximum, where old readings expire from the far end. Not a monotonic stack: it removes from one end only, so readings that slid out stay inside.

cards.q: Adjacent buildings of unit width have heights `h[i]`. Find the largest rectangular billboard that fits entirely inside their combined silhouette.
cards.a: Monotonic stack. Signal: each height's best rectangle spreads until the first shorter building on both sides. Key step: keep heights increasing, and when a height pops, its width spans from the new top to the current index.

cards.q: Each record stores the address of the next record, and a corrupted link may loop back. Detect this with O(1) extra memory.
cards.a: Fast and slow pointers on a linked list. Signal: a `next` chain, a possible loop, and no memory for a visited set. Not a visited set: it works but takes O(n) memory, which breaks the limit.

cards.q: A one-way chain of tracks has unknown length. In one pass, remove the track that is `k` from the end.
cards.a: Two pointers with a fixed gap, plus a dummy head. Signal: a position measured from the end of a one-way chain. Not count then walk: that takes two passes, while a lead `k` nodes ahead leaves the trail just before the target.

cards.q: A network of routers has no cycles. Find the pair of routers with the most hops between them.
cards.a: Tree DFS returning height. Signal: connected with no cycles, so the longest path bends at one top node. Not a search from every router: that is O(n^2), while one DFS adding the two tallest child heights at each node is O(n).

cards.q: A company hierarchy stores only manager-to-report links. Find the most junior person who sits at or above both of two given employees.
cards.a: Tree DFS for the lowest common ancestor. Signal: a shared ancestor, with links that only go downward. Not walking up from each employee: there are no parent links, so one DFS reports upward what each branch found.

cards.q: You have the pre-order and in-order visit sequences of a hierarchy with unique labels. Rebuild the hierarchy.
cards.a: Divide and conquer on the root. Signal: the first pre-order label is the root, and it splits the in-order sequence into left and right parts. Not a linear scan for each root: that is O(n^2) on a chain, while a hashmap from label to in-order index gives O(n).

cards.q: In a list of `n` = 1e5 exam scores, count the pairs where an earlier score is greater than a later one.
cards.a: Merge-based divide and conquer. Signal: counting out-of-order pairs, which split neatly into left, right and across. Not all pairs: O(n^2) at 1e5 is far too slow, while each merge counts the across pairs in linear time.

cards.q: A huge, very deep folder hierarchy must be searched for the match closest to the root.
cards.a: Level-order BFS. Signal: nearest by depth, so the first level with a match ends the search. Not DFS: its first match may be far deeper than the nearest one, so it cannot stop early.

cards.q: Print a company hierarchy rank by rank, one line per rank, from the CEO down.
cards.a: Level-order BFS. Signal: output grouped by distance from the root. Not a plain BFS loop: you lose where each rank ends unless you read `q.size()` at the start of each round.

cards.q: A search index stores keys in nodes where everything to a node's left must be smaller and everything to its right larger. Confirm that a given structure obeys the rule.
cards.a: BST validation with inherited bounds, or an in-order walk that must be strictly increasing. Signal: the rule covers whole sides, not just direct children. Not comparing with children only: a deep node can violate a bound set by a distant ancestor.

cards.q: Seats become free during a show, and each request asks for the lowest free seat number at or above `x`. Frees and requests are mixed, 1e5 of each.
cards.a: Ordered set with `lower_bound`, a balanced BST. Signal: successor queries mixed with insertions. Not binary search on a vector: the search is O(log n), but each insertion shifts O(n) elements.

cards.q: A search box must suggest stored product names as each letter is typed.
cards.a: Trie. Signal: queries about how a name begins, answered one character at a time. Not a hash set: it answers only whole-name lookups, so each keystroke would scan all names.

cards.q: Given a letter-tile board and a dictionary of 30000 words, find every word that can be traced through adjacent tiles.
cards.a: Trie plus backtracking. Signal: many words share their beginnings, so a single walk can track them all. Not one search per word: it repeats the same paths, while the trie abandons a path as soon as no word continues it.

cards.q: Scores arrive in an endless stream, and at any moment you must report the current 100th-highest score.
cards.a: Min-heap of size 100. Signal: a live stream with repeated top-k reads. Not quickselect: it needs all the data in memory and a rerun per query, while each new score here costs O(log k).

cards.q: Forty log files are each in timestamp order. Produce one combined file in timestamp order, with `N` lines in total.
cards.a: K-way merge with a min-heap. Signal: many already ordered inputs and a repeated need for the smallest head. Not concatenating and re-sorting: that costs O(N log N), while a heap of `k` heads costs O(N log k).

cards.q: Patient wait times are logged one at a time, and a dashboard shows the middle value after every new entry.
cards.a: Two heaps. Signal: a running median over a growing stream. Key step: a max-heap holds the lower half and a min-heap the upper half, rebalanced so their sizes differ by at most one.

cards.q: Split a class into two teams so that no two students who dislike each other share a team, or report that it is impossible.
cards.a: Two-colouring by BFS or DFS. Signal: two groups with 'must differ' constraints on pairs. Key step: give each neighbour the opposite colour, and a neighbour that already has your colour proves it impossible.

cards.q: On a metro map, every ride between adjacent stations counts as one stop. Find the fewest stops between two stations.
cards.a: Plain BFS. Signal: every edge costs the same. Not Dijkstra: it gives the same answer, but its heap adds a log factor, because BFS already reaches nodes in distance order.

cards.q: On a metro map, each ride between adjacent stations has its own positive travel time. Find the quickest trip between two stations.
cards.a: Dijkstra with a priority queue. Signal: non-negative weights that differ between edges. Not plain BFS: it minimises the number of rides, and a route with more rides can be quicker.

cards.q: A maze has locked doors and matching keys on the floor, and every move costs one step. Find the fewest steps to the exit.
cards.a: BFS over `(cell, keys bitmask)`. Signal: moves all cost 1, but what you can do depends on what you hold. Not Dijkstra: equal weights make its heap pointless, and the real fix is widening the state.

cards.q: Flights have different prices and you may use at most `k` connections. Find the cheapest way from city A to city B.
cards.a: Bellman-Ford limited to `k + 1` rounds, or Dijkstra over `(city, flights used)`. Signal: weighted edges plus a cap on edge count. Not plain Dijkstra on cities: the cheapest way into a city may spend too many flights, so one distance per city loses valid routes.

cards.q: Some road segments pay a rebate, so their cost is negative, though no loop makes money. Find the cheapest cost from the depot to every stop.
cards.a: Bellman-Ford, O(VE). Signal: negative edges with no negative cycle. Not Dijkstra: a settled node can still improve through a later negative edge, which breaks its greedy order.

cards.q: Possible fibre routes between offices each have a cost. Connect all the offices at the lowest total cable cost.
cards.a: Minimum spanning tree, Kruskal or Prim. Signal: connect everything at least total cost, with no source node. Not Dijkstra: it minimises distance from one source, which can cost more total cable.

cards.q: Each village can dig its own well at a given cost or lay a pipe to another village at a given cost. Supply water to all villages as cheaply as possible.
cards.a: Minimum spanning tree with a virtual node. Signal: every item can connect to others or pay a standalone cost. Key step: add a source node linked to each village by its well cost, then run Kruskal.

cards.q: An installer must place packages so that each comes after those it needs. Output any valid install order.
cards.a: Topological sort with Kahn's algorithm. Signal: 'before' constraints between items, and any valid order is accepted. Not DFS pre-order: it can list a package before another of its dependencies has been placed.

cards.q: Build targets list the targets they directly depend on. Decide whether any circular dependency exists.
cards.a: Topological sort, or DFS with three colours. Signal: directed dependency edges and a cycle check. Not union-find: it ignores direction, so the acyclic edges `a->b`, `a->c`, `b->c` look like a cycle.

cards.q: Cables are added one by one between routers, and between additions you must say whether two given routers can reach each other.
cards.a: Union-find. Signal: edges only get added, mixed with connectivity queries. Not BFS per query: O(V + E) per query is too slow, while each union or find is nearly O(1) amortised.

cards.q: Undirected cables are laid one at a time between routers. Report the first cable that closes a loop.
cards.a: Union-find. Signal: a loop appears exactly when a new undirected edge joins two already connected nodes. Not topological sort: it applies to directed graphs, and these edges have no direction.

cards.q: A satellite image marks each cell as forest or clear. Count the separate forests, where cells join only up, down, left and right.
cards.a: Flood fill by DFS or BFS. Signal: connected regions on cells with four neighbours. Not union-find: it works too, but one flood fill per unvisited cell is shorter and also O(rows * cols).

cards.q: Some cells of a warehouse floor plan hold mould, and each minute it spreads to the four adjacent cells. When is every reachable cell infected?
cards.a: Multi-source BFS. Signal: many origins spreading at one step per tick. Not a BFS from each source: that costs O(sources * cells), while starting all sources at distance 0 costs O(cells).

cards.q: Given coin types, list every distinct combination of coins that makes exactly `T`.
cards.a: Backtracking. Signal: the output is the full list of solutions. Not DP: merging states gives a count or a best value, but listing must still write out every solution.

cards.q: Given coin types, count the distinct combinations of coins that make exactly `T`, modulo 1e9+7.
cards.a: Unbounded knapsack DP. Signal: only a count is wanted, and subproblems `(coin index, remaining)` overlap. Not backtracking: it walks each combination, and the count can be astronomically large.

cards.q: A pizza shop offers 12 toppings. Enumerate every possible pizza, where topping order makes no difference.
cards.a: Subset enumeration: include or skip each item. Signal: order is irrelevant, so there are `2^n` results. Not permutations: they list the same pizza once per ordering of its toppings.

cards.q: A courier wants to try every possible visiting sequence of 9 shops, each visited once.
cards.a: Permutation enumeration with a `used` array. Signal: order matters and each item appears once, so there are `n!` results. Not subsets: include-or-skip fixes membership only and can never produce a different ordering.

cards.q: A courier must visit 18 shops once each with the least total driving time.
cards.a: Bitmask DP (Held-Karp). Signal: `n` near 20 and the state is the set visited plus the current shop. Not trying all orders: `18!` is hopeless, while `dp[mask][last]` costs O(2^n * n^2).

cards.q: Assign 16 workers to 16 jobs, one job each, minimising the total from a cost table.
cards.a: Bitmask DP. Signal: `n` around 15 to 20 with a one-to-one matching. Not trying all assignments: `16!` is hopeless, while `dp[mask]` over taken jobs costs O(2^n * n).

cards.q: A busker can play any of `n` festival days, each with a known tip, but must rest the day after playing. Maximise total tips.
cards.a: Linear DP. Signal: choose or skip each item, where a choice blocks its neighbour. Not greedy by largest tip: with tips 2, 3, 2 the greedy pick earns 3, while skipping it earns 4.

cards.q: From `n` = 1e5 daily record heights, keep as many days as possible, not necessarily adjacent, so the heights strictly rise.
cards.a: LIS with a `tails` array and `lower_bound`. Signal: longest increasing subsequence at a size where O(n^2) DP fails. Key step: `tails[k]` holds the smallest end value of any rising subsequence of length `k + 1`, giving O(n log n).

cards.q: A sequence of daily gains and losses is given. Find the best total over any consecutive period.
cards.a: Kadane's algorithm, a linear DP. Signal: best contiguous total with negatives allowed. Not sliding window: with negatives no rule says when to shrink, while `cur = max(x, cur + x)` restarts at the right moment.

cards.q: A rover crosses a warehouse from top-left to bottom-right moving only right or down, collecting the value in each cell. Maximise the total.
cards.a: Grid DP. Signal: moves only right and down, so dependencies have no cycles. Not greedy by best next cell: a poor step now can open a much richer region.

cards.q: Count the right-and-down routes from corner to corner of an `R` by `C` warehouse floor with some blocked cells, with `R` and `C` up to 1000.
cards.a: Grid DP. Signal: counting monotone routes, and blocked cells rule out a formula. Not DFS over routes: the count is exponential, while each cell just adds the two cells that feed it, for O(R * C).

cards.q: Count the right-and-down routes across an open `R` by `C` floor with no obstacles, where `R` and `C` reach 1e6, modulo 1e9+7.
cards.a: Combinatorics: `C(R + C - 2, R - 1)`. Signal: no obstacles, so every route is just an arrangement of right and down moves. Not cell-by-cell DP: 1e12 cells is too many, while factorials and modular inverses need only O(R + C) setup.

cards.q: Compute `a^b mod p` where `b` can reach 1e18.
cards.a: Fast exponentiation by squaring. Signal: a huge exponent under a modulus. Not repeated multiplication: `b` steps can never finish, while squaring and halving `b` takes O(log b).

cards.q: A spell checker ranks dictionary words by the fewest single-letter inserts, deletes and replacements needed to reach them from the typed word.
cards.a: Edit distance DP. Signal: aligning two sequences under per-character operations. Not a fixed rule per mismatch: the best operation depends on later letters, so `dp[i][j]` tries insert, delete and replace.

cards.q: Two playlists share many tracks. Find the longest list of tracks that appears in both in the same relative order, gaps allowed.
cards.a: Longest common subsequence DP. Signal: two sequences, order kept, gaps allowed. Not a sliding window: it handles contiguous runs only, and gaps need `dp[i][j]` over both positions.

cards.q: A URL slug lost its hyphens. Decide whether it can be cut into valid dictionary words.
cards.a: DP over cut positions. Signal: `dp[i]` depends only on whether a dictionary word ends at `i` from a reachable cut. Not greedy longest match: with words `a`, `ab`, `bc`, the text `abc` fails if you take `ab` first.

cards.q: Split `n` parcels between two trucks so both carry exactly the same weight, with total weight at most 20000.
cards.a: 0/1 knapsack on reachable sums (subset sum). Signal: a target of half the total, with small integer weights. Key step: loop sums downward in `dp[s] |= dp[s - w]`, so each parcel counts at most once.

cards.q: A vending machine has coin values such as 1, 3 and 4. Give exact change for `T` with the fewest coins.
cards.a: Unbounded knapsack DP. Signal: arbitrary coin values and a minimum count. Not greedy by largest coin: for 6 it pays 4 + 1 + 1, while 3 + 3 uses two coins.

cards.q: Neighbouring clusters on a line merge two at a time, each merge costing the combined size of the pair. Find the cheapest way to merge everything into one.
cards.a: Interval DP. Signal: only adjacent pieces combine, so the last merge splits the range in two. Not the Huffman greedy: it merges the two smallest anywhere, which adjacency forbids.

cards.q: Clusters merge two at a time, any two you choose, each merge costing the combined size of the pair. Find the cheapest way to merge everything into one.
cards.a: Greedy with a min-heap (Huffman). Signal: any pair may merge, so the two smallest always go first. Not interval DP: there is no adjacency, so no ranges to split, and the heap gives O(n log n).

cards.q: A 100 cm bar must be cut at `m` marked points, and each cut costs the length of the piece being cut. Find the cheapest cutting order.
cards.a: Interval DP over cut positions. Signal: the order of operations matters and each one splits a range. Key step: `dp[i][j]` tries every cut `k` between marks `i` and `j` as the first, paying `pos[j] - pos[i]` plus both sides.

cards.q: Employees form a hierarchy with a fun score each, and nobody attends the party along with their direct manager. Maximise the total fun.
cards.a: Tree DP with two states per node. Signal: a take-or-skip rule along parent-child links. Key step: `take = fun + sum(skip(child))` and `skip = sum(max(take(child), skip(child)))`.

cards.q: In a network of `n` routers with no cycles, compute for every router the total hop count to all the others.
cards.a: Tree DP with rerooting. Signal: a whole-network answer is wanted at every node. Key step: solve one root, then moving to child `c` changes the total by `n - 2 * size[c]`, for O(n) overall.

cards.q: A trader holds at most one unit of a commodity, and after each sale the rules ban buying for one day. Given daily prices, find the best total profit.
cards.a: State machine DP. Signal: today's allowed action depends on a small set of modes: holding, just sold, free. Not collecting every rise: the ban makes adjacent trades conflict, so each day must update all modes.

cards.q: A trader can buy and sell a commodity on any days with no fees, holding at most one unit. Given daily prices, find the best total profit.
cards.a: Greedy sum of rises. Signal: no limit on trades, so every price rise can be collected. Not state machine DP: it also works, but `ans += max(0, p[i] - p[i - 1])` is all you need.

cards.q: Count passcodes of length `n` over three symbols in which no symbol appears three times in a row.
cards.a: State machine DP. Signal: validity depends only on a short tail of the sequence. Not listing all codes: `3^n` grows too fast, while states `(last symbol, run length)` keep a fixed number of counts per position.

cards.q: From each tile you may leap forward up to `r[i]` tiles. Can you get from the first tile to the last?
cards.a: Greedy farthest reach. Signal: a yes/no question where only the best reach so far matters. Not DP over predecessors: it costs O(n^2), when one running maximum decides it in O(n).

cards.q: Every sensor id in a log appears exactly twice except one. Find that id with O(1) extra memory.
cards.a: XOR of all values. Signal: pairs cancel, and the memory limit rules out storing anything. Not a hash set: it needs O(n) memory.

cards.q: Each of 1e6 users holds up to 32 fixed permissions, and each check asks whether a user has every permission in a required set.
cards.a: Bitmask. Signal: a small fixed universe of flags with set operations. Not per-user sets of names: each check costs far more than the O(1) test `(user & need) == need`.

cards.q: Check whether a 1 MB text contains a given 10 KB signature, with a guaranteed linear worst case.
cards.a: KMP. Signal: one needle, one haystack and a linear worst-case bound. Not `string::find`: typical implementations are O(nm) in the worst case on repetitive input.

cards.q: Find any block of `L` characters that appears at least twice in a document of 1e6 characters.
cards.a: Rolling hash (Rabin-Karp). Signal: many overlapping fixed-length blocks to compare. Not `substr` into a hash set: each key costs O(L), so O(nL) overall, while a rolling hash shifts in O(1) and verifies on a hit.

cards.q: A live table of `n` teams receives score changes, and each query asks for the lowest score between two table positions.
cards.a: Segment tree. Signal: point updates mixed with range minimum. Not a Fenwick tree: min has no inverse, so you cannot subtract two prefix answers to isolate a range.

cards.q: A cache holds `C` entries and evicts the one used longest ago. `get` and `put` must both be O(1).
cards.a: Hash map plus doubly linked list. Signal: O(1) lookup combined with O(1) move-to-front by recency. Not an ordered map on timestamps: it adds a log factor to every access.

cards.q: A raffle holds a changing set of names. Adding, removing and drawing a uniformly random name must all be O(1) on average.
cards.a: Vector plus hash map from name to index. Signal: a random draw needs positions, and removal needs lookup by name. Key step: to remove, swap the item with the last slot, fix its index, then `pop_back`.

cards.q: A robot on a bounded board obeys 1000 commands: turn left, turn right, or step forward unless a wall blocks it. Report where it ends.
cards.a: Direct simulation. Signal: the rules are spelled out and the limits are small, so no clever idea is needed. Not hunting for a formula: the outcome depends on the whole command order, so run it with `dx`, `dy` and a direction index.

cards.q: A board game state evolves by a fixed rule each tick, and you need the state after 1e12 ticks. Only a few thousand distinct states can occur.
cards.a: Simulation with cycle detection. Signal: deterministic steps, a small state space and a huge step count. Key step: record when each state first appears, then jump with `%` on the remaining ticks.

cards.q: Write `int firstTrue(int n, function<bool(int)> pred)`, where `pred` is false then true over `[0, n)`. Return the first index where `pred` is true, or `n` if none.
cards.a: Invariant: every index below `lo` is false and every index at or above `hi` is true. A true `mid` sets `hi = mid`, a false one sets `lo = mid + 1`, and `lo == hi` at the end is the answer.

cards.q: Write `int lowerBound(const vector<int>& a, int target)` for sorted `a`. Return the first index with `a[i] >= target`, or `a.size()` if none.
cards.a: The predicate is `a[mid] >= target`, never `==`. The result can be `n`, so check `lo < n` before reading `a[lo]`.

cards.q: Write `int upperBound(const vector<int>& a, int target)` for sorted `a`. Return the first index with `a[i] > target`, or `a.size()` if none.
cards.a: Only the predicate changes from lower bound: `>` instead of `>=`. `upperBound - lowerBound` is the number of copies of `target`.

cards.q: This binary search hangs on some inputs. Which condition is wrong, and why?
cards.a: `while (lo <= hi)`. When `lo == hi` and `pred(mid)` is true, `hi = mid` changes nothing and the loop never ends. The half-open form stops at `lo == hi`, so it needs `lo < hi`.

cards.q: Write `bool fits(const vector<int>& w, int k, int cap)` and `int minCapacity(const vector<int>& w, int k)` for non-empty `w`, `k >= 1`, and a total below `INT_MAX`. Return the smallest `cap` that splits `w`, in order, into at most `k` contiguous groups with each sum `<= cap`.
cards.a: `lo` starts at the largest item, because a smaller `cap` cannot hold it. `hi` is one past the largest candidate, the total, because the range is half-open.

cards.q: Write `int intSqrt(int x)` for `x >= 0`. Return the largest `r` with `r * r <= x`.
cards.a: To find the last true, search for the first false and return `lo - 1`. Use `long long`, because `mid * mid` overflows `int`.

cards.q: Write `int findMinIndex(const vector<int>& a)` for a non-empty sorted array of distinct values, rotated by any amount. Return the index of the minimum.
cards.a: Compare with the last element, not the first: `a[i] <= a[n - 1]` is false on the left part and true from the minimum onward. It also holds with no rotation at all.

cards.q: Write `int searchRotated(const vector<int>& a, int target)` for a sorted array of distinct values, rotated by any amount. Return the index of `target`, or -1 if absent.
cards.a: `pred(i)` means position `i` is at or after `target`, which makes the rotated array monotonic again. Values on the same side of the rotation compare directly; otherwise the side alone decides.

cards.q: Write `pair<int, int> twoSumSorted(const vector<int>& a, int target)` for sorted `a`. Return indices `{l, r}` with `l < r` and `a[l] + a[r] == target`, or `{-1, -1}` if none.
cards.a: A sum that is too small can only grow by moving `l` up, and one that is too large can only shrink by moving `r` down. Each step discards a value that cannot be part of any answer.

cards.q: Write `int removeDuplicates(vector<int>& a)` for sorted `a`. Compact the distinct values to the front in place and return how many there are.
cards.a: Invariant: `a[0..k)` holds the distinct values seen so far. The next value is kept only if it differs from `a[k - 1]`.

cards.q: Write `vector<vector<int>> threeSum(vector<int> a)`. Return every distinct triple of values that sums to 0, each listed once.
cards.a: Skip repeats in two places: `i` against `a[i - 1]`, and `l` after a hit. `r` needs no skip, because the larger `a[l]` makes the old `a[r]` overshoot and `r` then moves on its own.

cards.q: Write `int maxWindowSum(const vector<int>& a, int k)` for `1 <= k <= a.size()`. Return the maximum sum over all contiguous windows of exactly `k` elements.
cards.a: Add `a[r]`, drop `a[r - k]` once `r >= k`, and record once `r >= k - 1`. That order keeps the recorded window at exactly `k` elements.

cards.q: Write `int longestUnique(const string& s)`. Return the length of the longest substring with no repeated character.
cards.a: Grow `r` every step, then shrink `l` until the window is valid again. Record after the shrink, when `[l, r]` is valid.

cards.q: Write `int minLenAtLeast(const vector<int>& a, int target)` for positive values and positive `target`. Return the length of the shortest contiguous subarray with sum `>= target`, or 0 if none.
cards.a: For a shortest window, record inside the `while`, shrinking for as long as the window stays valid. Positive values are what make the sum grow and shrink with the window.

cards.q: Write `long long countAtMost(const vector<int>& a, int k)` for `k >= 0`. Return how many contiguous subarrays have at most `k` distinct values.
cards.a: A valid window `[l, r]` gives `r - l + 1` subarrays ending at `r`, so add that every step. For exactly `k` distinct, use `countAtMost(a, k) - countAtMost(a, k - 1)`.

cards.q: Write `int countSumK(const vector<int>& a, int k)`, where `a` may hold negatives. Return how many contiguous subarrays sum to `k`.
cards.a: Seed `cnt[0] = 1` for subarrays that start at index 0. Query `sum - k` before adding `sum`, or `k == 0` counts an empty subarray.

cards.q: Write `vector<int> rangeAdd(int n, const vector<array<int, 3>>& ops)`, where each op `{l, r, x}` adds `x` to indices `l` through `r` of an all-zero array of size `n`. Return the final array.
cards.a: `diff` needs size `n + 1` so that `r + 1` stays in bounds. Each op is O(1), and one running sum at the end rebuilds the array.

cards.q: Write `vector<int> nextGreater(const vector<int>& a)`. For each index, return the index of the next strictly greater element to its right, or -1 if none.
cards.a: The stack holds indices still waiting for an answer, with non-increasing values. Store indices, not values, because you must write `ans[st.top()]`.

cards.q: Write `int largestRectangle(vector<int> h)` for non-negative bar heights. Return the largest rectangle area inside the histogram.
cards.a: The sentinel 0 at the end flushes the stack. After a pop, the new top is the nearest smaller bar on the left, so the width is `i - l - 1`.

cards.q: Write `vector<int> windowMax(const vector<int>& a, int k)` for `1 <= k <= a.size()`. Return the maximum of each contiguous window of size `k`, left to right.
cards.a: The deque holds indices with strictly decreasing values, so the front is the window maximum. Evict smaller values from the back, and evict the front once `dq.front() <= i - k`.

cards.q: With `ListNode` (`val`, `next`), write `ListNode* reverseList(ListNode* head)`. Reverse the list iteratively and return the new head.
cards.a: Save `cur->next` before overwriting it. When the loop ends `cur` is null, so the new head is `prev`.

cards.q: With `ListNode` (`val`, `next`), write `ListNode* middleNode(ListNode* head)`. Return the middle node, or the second of the two middles when the length is even.
cards.a: Loop on `fast && fast->next`, testing `fast` first. `fast` moves twice as far, so `slow` is at the middle when `fast` runs out.

cards.q: With `ListNode` (`val`, `next`, constructor `ListNode(int x)`), write `ListNode* mergeLists(ListNode* a, ListNode* b)`. Merge two sorted lists by relinking nodes and return the merged head.
cards.a: The dummy node removes the special case for the first append, so return `dummy.next`. When one list ends, one link attaches the rest of the other.

cards.q: With `ListNode` (`val`, `next`), write `bool hasCycle(ListNode* head)`. Return whether the list contains a cycle, using O(1) extra space.
cards.a: Compare after moving, because both pointers start equal at `head`. Inside a cycle `fast` gains one step per round, so the two must meet.

cards.q: With `ListNode` (`val`, `next`, constructor `ListNode(int x)`), write `ListNode* removeNthFromEnd(ListNode* head, int k)`. Unlink the `k`-th node from the end, for valid `k`, and return the head.
cards.a: The dummy covers the case where the head itself is removed. Start both pointers at the dummy, `k` apart, so `slow` stops just before the target.

cards.q: With `TreeNode` (`val`, `left`, `right`), write `void preorder(TreeNode* node, vector<int>& out)`. Append the values in node, left, right order.
cards.a: `out` must be a reference, or every call appends to its own copy.

cards.q: With `TreeNode` (`val`, `left`, `right`), write `void inorder(TreeNode* node, vector<int>& out)`. Append the values in left, node, right order.
cards.a: On a BST this order gives the values sorted, which is the fact most problems use.

cards.q: With `TreeNode` (`val`, `left`, `right`), write `void postorder(TreeNode* node, vector<int>& out)`. Append the values in left, right, node order.
cards.a: Children finish before the parent, which is why subtree answers such as height are computed in this order.

cards.q: With `TreeNode` (`val`, `left`, `right`), write `vector<int> inorderIter(TreeNode* root)`. Return the in-order values using an explicit stack.
cards.a: Loop while `cur || !st.empty()`. Push the whole left spine, pop and visit one node, then move to its right child.

cards.q: With `TreeNode` (`val`, `left`, `right`), write `int height(TreeNode* node, int& best)` and `int diameter(TreeNode* root)`. Return the largest number of edges on any path between two nodes.
cards.a: The recursion returns one thing and records another: it returns the height, a single branch, while `best` tracks the path through both branches.

cards.q: With `TreeNode` (`val`, `left`, `right`), write `vector<vector<int>> levelOrder(TreeNode* root)`. Return the values grouped by depth, top to bottom and left to right.
cards.a: Save `q.size()` in `sz` before the inner loop, because the children pushed during the loop change the size.

cards.q: With `TreeNode` (`val`, `left`, `right`), write `bool validate(TreeNode* node, long long lo, long long hi)` and `bool isValidBST(TreeNode* root)`. Return whether the tree is a strict BST, with every value inside the open range `(lo, hi)`.
cards.a: Comparing a node only with its children is the classic bug, because a whole subtree must respect every ancestor. The bounds are `long long` so that node values of `INT_MIN` and `INT_MAX` still pass.

cards.q: With `TreeNode` (`val`, `left`, `right`, constructor `TreeNode(int x)`), write `TreeNode* insertBST(TreeNode* root, int x)`. Insert `x`, which is not yet in the tree, and return the root.
cards.a: Assign the recursive result back to `root->left` or `root->right`, because that is what links the new leaf. Return `root` at every level.

cards.q: Define `struct TrieNode` with `TrieNode* next[26]` and `bool isEnd`, both default-initialised, then write `void insert(TrieNode* root, const string& word)` for lowercase words.
cards.a: `= {}` zeroes the child pointers, and without it they hold garbage. Set `isEnd` on the last node after the loop, not on the root.

cards.q: With `TrieNode` (`next[26]`, `isEnd`), write `bool search(TrieNode* root, const string& word)` for lowercase words. Return whether `word` was inserted as a whole word.
cards.a: Return `cur->isEnd`, not `true`, or any stored prefix counts as a word. A prefix check is the same loop ending in `return true`.

cards.q: Write `vector<int> topK(const vector<int>& a, int k)` for `k >= 1`. Return the `k` largest values in ascending order, in O(n log k) with a heap.
cards.a: Use a min-heap capped at size `k`. Its root is the smallest of the best `k`, so it is the one to evict.

cards.q: Write `struct MedianFinder` with `priority_queue<int> lo`, a min-heap `hi`, `void add(int x)` and `double median()`. `lo` holds the smaller half plus any odd element, and `median` is only called after an `add`.
cards.a: Every `x` passes through `lo` and then `hi`, which keeps all of `lo` at or below all of `hi`. Then rebalance so `lo` is never the smaller heap.

cards.q: Write `vector<int> mergeK(const vector<vector<int>>& lists)` for sorted lists, using a min-heap of `{value, list index, element index}` tuples. Return all values in sorted order.
cards.a: The heap holds at most one entry per list, so each step costs O(log k). Skip empty lists when seeding.

cards.q: Write `void dfs(vector<string>& grid, int r, int c)` and `int countIslands(vector<string>& grid)` for a non-empty grid of `'1'` land and `'0'` water. Return the number of 4-connected land regions.
cards.a: Test bounds before reading the cell, at the top of `dfs`. Overwrite `'1'` with `'0'` before recursing, or the recursion never ends.

cards.q: Write `int shortestPath(const vector<string>& grid, int sr, int sc, int tr, int tc)` with `'#'` as walls and a non-wall start. Return the fewest 4-directional steps from `(sr, sc)` to `(tr, tc)`, or -1 if unreachable.
cards.a: Set `dist` when a cell is pushed, not when it is popped, or the same cell enters the queue many times. A `dist` of -1 doubles as the unvisited mark.

cards.q: Write `vector<vector<int>> nearestSource(const vector<vector<int>>& grid)`, where cells equal to 1 are sources. Return each cell's 4-directional step distance to its nearest source, or all -1 if the grid has none.
cards.a: Push every source at distance 0 before the loop. The queue then expands all sources in lockstep, so the first visit to a cell is the shortest.

cards.q: Write `vector<vector<int>> buildGraph(int n, const vector<pair<int, int>>& edges)` for an undirected graph on nodes `0` to `n - 1`. Return the adjacency list.
cards.a: Undirected means two pushes per edge; a directed graph has only `adj[u].push_back(v)`. Size `adj` with `n` so isolated nodes still get an empty list.

cards.q: Write `vector<int> topoSort(int n, const vector<vector<int>>& adj)` for a directed graph, using Kahn's algorithm. Return a topological order, or an empty vector if the graph has a cycle.
cards.a: A node enters the queue exactly when its in-degree reaches 0. Nodes on a cycle never reach 0, so `order` ends up shorter than `n`.

cards.q: Write `bool dfs(int u, const vector<vector<int>>& adj, vector<int>& color)` and `bool hasCycle(int n, const vector<vector<int>>& adj)` with colours 0 unvisited, 1 on the current path, 2 finished. Return whether the directed graph has a cycle.
cards.a: Reaching a colour 1 node is a back edge, which means a cycle. Colour 2 nodes are finished and safe to skip, a distinction a plain `visited` flag cannot make.

cards.q: Write `struct DSU` with `vector<int> parent, sz`, a constructor `DSU(int n)`, `int find(int x)` and `bool unite(int a, int b)`. `find` compresses paths, and `unite` joins by size and returns false if `a` and `b` were already together.
cards.a: Link roots, never the original `a` and `b`, so reassign both with `find` first. Hang the smaller root under the larger and add its size.

cards.q: Write `vector<int> dijkstra(int n, const vector<vector<pair<int, int>>>& adj, int src)`, where `adj[u]` holds `{v, w}` with `w >= 0`. Return the shortest distance from `src` to every node, with `INT_MAX` for unreachable nodes.
cards.a: Skip stale entries with `if (d > dist[u]) continue;`, because a node can sit in the heap several times. Heap entries are `{dist, node}`, so that pairs order by distance.

cards.q: Write `int bellmanFord(int n, const vector<array<int, 3>>& edges, int src, int dst, int k)`, where each edge is `{u, v, w}`. Return the cheapest cost from `src` to `dst` using at most `k` edges, or `INT_MAX` if there is no such path.
cards.a: Relax from a copy of the previous round, so that each round adds at most one edge. Skip `prev[u] == INT_MAX`, or `prev[u] + w` overflows.

cards.q: Using `DSU` with `unite`, write `int kruskal(int n, vector<array<int, 3>> edges)`, where each edge is `{w, u, v}`. Return the weight of a minimum spanning tree, or -1 if the graph is disconnected.
cards.a: Putting `w` first lets a plain `sort` order the edges by weight. `unite` returning false means the edge would close a cycle, so it is skipped.

cards.q: Write `void dfs(const vector<int>& a, int start, vector<int>& cur, vector<vector<int>>& ans)` and `vector<vector<int>> subsets(const vector<int>& a)` for distinct values. Return all subsets.
cards.a: Record `cur` on entry, because every node of the recursion tree is a subset. Looping from `start` stops an element being reused or reordered.

cards.q: Write `void dfs(const vector<int>& a, vector<bool>& used, vector<int>& cur, vector<vector<int>>& ans)` and `vector<vector<int>> permutations(const vector<int>& a)` for distinct values. Return all permutations.
cards.a: The loop restarts at 0 on every call, so `used` is what prevents repeats. Undo both `cur.push_back` and `used[i] = true` after the recursive call.

cards.q: Write `void dfs(int n, int k, int start, vector<int>& cur, vector<vector<int>>& ans)` and `vector<vector<int>> combinations(int n, int k)`. Return all `k`-element subsets of `1` to `n`.
cards.a: Recurse with `x + 1`, so each choice only looks forward. That produces every combination exactly once, in increasing order.

cards.q: Write `void dfs(const vector<int>& a, int start, int remain, vector<int>& cur, vector<vector<int>>& ans)` and `vector<vector<int>> combinationSum(vector<int> a, int target)` for positive values with possible duplicates. Return each distinct combination that sums to `target`, using each element at most once.
cards.a: Sort first, then skip with `i > start && a[i] == a[i - 1]`: equal values may not open two branches at the same depth. Writing `i > 0` is the bug, because it also forbids equal values along one path.

cards.q: Write `int maxNonAdjacent(const vector<int>& a)` for non-negative values. Return the largest sum of elements with no two adjacent, in O(1) extra space.
cards.a: `prev1` is the best answer up to the previous element and `prev2` up to the one before it. Each element is either skipped (`prev1`) or taken (`prev2 + x`).

cards.q: Write `int minPathSum(const vector<vector<int>>& grid)` for a non-empty grid of non-negative values, moving only right or down. Return the smallest path sum from top-left to bottom-right, using a table with one extra row and column.
cards.a: Border cells stay `INT_MAX` so `min` ignores them, and `dp[0][1] = 0` seeds the start. The padding shifts indices, so `dp[i][j]` reads `grid[i - 1][j - 1]`.

cards.q: Write `int lengthOfLIS(const vector<int>& a)` in O(n log n) with patience sorting. Return the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence.
cards.a: `tails[i]` is the smallest possible last value of an increasing subsequence of length `i + 1`. Only its size is meaningful, because `tails` itself need not be a real subsequence. `lower_bound` gives strictly increasing.

cards.q: Write `int lcs(const string& s, const string& t)`. Return the length of the longest common subsequence.
cards.a: `dp[i][j]` covers the first `i` chars of `s` and the first `j` of `t`, so the chars compared are `s[i - 1]` and `t[j - 1]`. Row 0 and column 0 stay zero for empty prefixes.

cards.q: Write `int editDistance(const string& s, const string& t)`. Return the fewest single-character inserts, deletes and replacements that turn `s` into `t`.
cards.a: Unlike LCS the borders are not zero: a prefix of length `i` needs `i` edits to match an empty string. Matching chars copy the diagonal at no cost.

cards.q: Write `int knapsack(const vector<int>& w, const vector<int>& v, int cap)` with a 1D `dp`, for items of weight `w[i]` and value `v[i]`. Return the best total value within capacity `cap`, using each item at most once.
cards.a: Loop the capacity downward, so `dp[c - w[i]]` still excludes item `i`. An upward loop lets the same item be taken twice.

cards.q: Write `int unboundedKnapsack(const vector<int>& w, const vector<int>& v, int cap)` with a 1D `dp`, for positive weights. Return the best total value within capacity `cap`, where each item may be used any number of times.
cards.a: Identical to the 0/1 form except that the capacity loop runs upward. `dp[c - w[i]]` may already include item `i`, which is exactly what allows repeats.

cards.q: Write `vector<vector<int>> mergeIntervals(vector<vector<int>> intervals)`, where each interval is `{start, end}`. Return the union as disjoint intervals sorted by start, joining intervals that touch.
cards.a: After sorting, only the last merged interval can overlap the next one. Take `max` for the new end, because the next interval may sit entirely inside the last.

cards.q: Write `int minMergeCost(const vector<int>& a)` for a non-empty row of piles, where merging two adjacent piles costs their combined size. Return the smallest total cost to merge everything into one pile.
cards.a: Loop on `len` first, so every shorter interval is ready. `k` splits `[i, j]` into `[i, k]` and `[k + 1, j]`, and the last merge always costs the sum of `[i, j]`.

cards.q: Write `int minAssignment(const vector<vector<int>>& cost)` for `n` workers and `n` jobs, where `cost[i][j]` is worker `i` doing job `j`. Return the smallest total cost, using a DP over the set of taken jobs.
cards.a: `mask` is the set of taken jobs, so the next worker is `__builtin_popcount(mask)`. Adding a bit makes the number larger, so looping masks upward finishes every subset first.

cards.q: Write `int dfs(int u, const vector<vector<int>>& adj, vector<int>& memo)` and `int longestPath(int n, const vector<vector<int>>& adj)` for a DAG, with -1 meaning not computed. Return the largest number of edges on any path.
cards.a: Read the memo on the first line and write it just before returning. `memo` must be a reference, or nothing is remembered and the run turns exponential. Use -1 as the sentinel, because 0 is a valid answer here.

cards.q: Write `int partition(vector<int>& a, int lo, int hi)` on the half-open range `[lo, hi)`, with `a[hi - 1]` as the pivot. Move smaller values left of the pivot and return its final index.
cards.a: `i` is the boundary: everything in `[lo, i)` is smaller than the pivot. The pivot waits at `hi - 1` during the scan and swaps into `i` at the end.

cards.q: Using `partition(a, lo, hi)` on the half-open range `[lo, hi)`, write `int quickselect(vector<int> a, int k)`. For distinct values, return the `k`-th smallest, 0-indexed, or -1 if `k` is out of range, in expected O(n).
cards.a: After `partition`, `a[p]` is in its final place, so only the side holding `k` remains. The random pivot is what avoids O(n^2) on sorted input.

cards.q: Write `void mergeSort(vector<int>& a, int lo, int hi)` on the half-open range `[lo, hi)`. Sort it stably, merging through a temporary vector.
cards.a: The base case is `hi - lo <= 1`, and the right half starts at `mid`, not `mid + 1`. Take from the left on `<=` to stay stable.

cards.q: Write `struct LRUCache` with `list<pair<int, int>> items` (most recent first), a map `pos` from key to list iterator, `LRUCache(int capacity)` for `capacity >= 1`, `int get(int key)` and `void put(int key, int value)`. `get` returns -1 for a missing key, and both run in O(1).
cards.a: `splice` moves a node without invalidating any iterator, so `pos` stays correct. On eviction, erase the key from `pos` before popping the list back.

cards.q: Write `long long power(long long base, long long exp, long long mod)` for `base >= 0`, `exp >= 0` and `1 < mod < 2^31`. Return `base^exp % mod` in O(log exp).
cards.a: Square `base` every step, and multiply it into `ans` only when the low bit of `exp` is set. Keeping `mod` below `2^31` keeps every product inside `long long`.

cards.q: Write `int gcd(int a, int b)` for non-negative inputs, using Euclid's algorithm. Return the greatest common divisor.
cards.a: `gcd(a, b)` equals `gcd(b, a % b)`, and the recursion stops at `b == 0` with the answer in `a`. C++17 also offers `gcd` in `<numeric>`.

cards.q: Write `vector<int> sieve(int n)` for `n >= 1`, using the sieve of Eratosthenes. Return all primes up to and including `n`.
cards.a: Start crossing off at `i * i`, because smaller multiples already have a smaller prime factor. Compute that start as `1LL * i * i`, or it overflows.

cards.q: Write `struct SegTree` with `int n`, `vector<int> t` of size `2 * n`, a constructor from `const vector<int>& a`, `void update(int i, int val)` and `int query(int l, int r)`. It is a bottom-up sum tree where `query` sums the half-open range `[l, r)`.
cards.a: Leaves live at `t[n + i]`, and the parent of `i` is `i / 2`. In `query`, an odd `l` takes `t[l++]` and an odd `r` takes `t[--r]` before both climb.

cards.q: Write `struct Fenwick` with `vector<int> t`, a constructor `Fenwick(int n)`, `void add(int i, int delta)` for a 0-based `i`, and `int prefix(int i)`. `prefix` returns the sum of the first `i` elements.
cards.a: The tree is 1-based inside, so `add` starts with `i++` and `t[0]` stays unused. `i & -i` is the lowest set bit: `add` climbs by it and `prefix` strips it. The sum of `[l, r)` is `prefix(r) - prefix(l)`.

cards.q: Write `vector<int> prefixFunction(const string& s)`. Return `pi`, where `pi[i]` is the length of the longest proper prefix of `s[0..i]` that is also its suffix.
cards.a: On a mismatch fall back with `k = pi[k - 1]`, never straight to 0. To find `pat` in `text`, run this on `pat + '#' + text` and look for a value equal to `pat.size()`.

cards.q: With file-level `const long long BASE = 131, MOD = 1000000007;`, write `struct StringHash` with `vector<long long> h, p`, a constructor from `const string& s`, and `long long get(int l, int r)`. `get` returns the polynomial hash of the half-open range `[l, r)`.
cards.a: `get` subtracts the prefix shifted by `r - l` places, and the result can be negative, so add `MOD` before the last `% MOD`. Equal hashes only suggest equal strings, so confirm a match when a collision would matter.

cards.q: Write `vector<int> reservoirSample(const vector<int>& stream, int k)` for `k <= stream.size()`, using `rand()`. Return `k` elements chosen uniformly at random, in one pass and O(k) extra space.
cards.a: Element `i`, 0-based, enters with probability `k / (i + 1)` and replaces a random slot. Every element then ends up in the sample with the same chance, `k / n`.

cards.q: Declare `pq`, a min-heap of `int`.
cards.a: The default `priority_queue<int>` is a max-heap. To pass `greater<int>` you must also spell out the container, `vector<int>`.
cards.code: priority_queue<int, vector<int>, greater<int>> pq;

cards.q: With `using P = pair<int, int>;`, declare a lambda `cmp` and a heap `pq` so the pair with the smallest `.second` is on top.
cards.a: A comparator returning true means `a` sinks below `b`, so `>` gives a min-heap. `decltype(cmp)` names the type, and C++17 also needs `cmp` passed to the constructor.
cards.code: auto cmp = [](const P& a, const P& b) { return a.second > b.second; }; priority_queue, decltype(cmp)> pq(cmp);

cards.q: Store in `int i` the index of the first element of sorted `v` that is not less than `x`.
cards.a: `lower_bound` returns an iterator, and subtracting `v.begin()` turns it into an index. If every element is smaller, `i` equals `v.size()`.
cards.code: int i = lower_bound(v.begin(), v.end(), x) - v.begin();

cards.q: Set `bool has` to whether key `k` is in map `m`, without modifying `m`.
cards.a: `m[k]` inserts a zero for a missing key, so testing with it grows the map.
cards.code: bool has = m.find(k) != m.end();

cards.q: In what order does a range-for visit a `map`, and in what order an `unordered_map`?
cards.a: `map` goes in ascending key order. `unordered_map` order is unspecified and can change after a rehash.

cards.q: For `map<int, int> m`, why write `m.lower_bound(k)` and not `std::lower_bound` over `m.begin()` to `m.end()`?
cards.a: The member function descends the tree in O(log n). `std::lower_bound` needs random-access iterators to be fast, so on a `map` it walks step by step in O(n). It also compares whole `pair` elements, so it would need a custom comparator.

cards.q: For `set<int> s`, set `ans` to the largest element `<= x`, leaving `ans` unchanged if there is none.
cards.a: `upper_bound` gives the first element `> x`, so the one before it is the floor. Check against `s.begin()`, because `prev(s.begin())` is undefined.
cards.code:
auto it = s.upper_bound(x);
if (it != s.begin()) ans = *prev(it);

cards.q: Insert `x` into `set<int> s` and set `bool added` to whether `x` was new.
cards.a: `insert` returns `pair<iterator, bool>`. The `bool` is false if an equal element already existed.
cards.code: bool added = s.insert(x).second;

cards.q: Set `int lo` and `int hi` to the smallest and largest values in non-empty `multiset<int> ms`.
cards.a: `set` and `multiset` stay sorted, so the two ends hold the extremes. Use `rbegin()`, because `end()` points past the last element.
cards.code:
int lo = *ms.begin();
int hi = *ms.rbegin();

cards.q: Remove exactly one copy of `x` from `multiset<int> ms`, where `x` is known to be present.
cards.a: `ms.erase(x)` removes every copy, because the value overload erases all matches. The iterator overload erases one, and passing `end()` is undefined.
cards.code: ms.erase(ms.find(x));

cards.q: Erase every entry of `map<int, int> m` with value 0, in a single loop over iterators.
cards.a: `erase` invalidates `it` and returns the next valid iterator. Advance either by that assignment or by `it++`, never both.

cards.q: Delete every element equal to `x` from `vector<int> v` in O(n).
cards.a: `remove` shifts the kept elements forward and returns the new logical end, without changing the size. `erase` then cuts off the tail.
cards.code: v.erase(remove(v.begin(), v.end(), x), v.end());

cards.q: Declare `dp`, a table of zeros with `m + 1` rows and `n + 1` columns.
cards.a: The second argument is one row, and the outer vector copies it `m + 1` times. `vector<int>(n + 1)` is already zero-filled.
cards.code: vector<vector<int>> dp(m + 1, vector<int>(n + 1));

cards.q: How many elements do `vector<int> a(3, 7);` and `vector<int> b{3, 7};` hold?
cards.a: `a` holds three 7s. `b` holds two elements, 3 and 7, because braces prefer the initializer-list constructor.

cards.q: After `vector<int> v; v.reserve(10);`, is `v[0] = 1;` valid?
cards.a: No, it is undefined. `reserve` only sets capacity, so the size is still 0, and `resize(10)` is what creates elements.

cards.q: Why does `auto& x = flags[0];` not compile for `vector<bool> flags`?
cards.a: `vector<bool>` packs elements into bits, so `operator[]` returns a temporary proxy object, not a `bool&`. A non-const reference cannot bind to a temporary.

cards.q: What does this print?
cards.a: `1`. `auto` deduces the proxy, which still refers to the bit. Write `bool x = flags[0];` to get a real copy.

cards.q: Why is the last line undefined behaviour?
cards.a: `push_back` may reallocate, which invalidates every reference, pointer and iterator into the vector. Take them after the last insertion, or hold an index instead.

cards.q: In `map`, `set` and `list`, which iterators does an insert or an erase invalidate?
cards.a: An insert invalidates none. An erase invalidates only iterators to the erased element.

cards.q: What does a rehash of an `unordered_map` invalidate?
cards.a: All iterators, but not pointers or references to elements. Any insert can trigger a rehash, so do not hold an iterator across one.

cards.q: Append the pair `(1, 2)` to `vector<pair<int, int>> v` using `emplace_back`.
cards.a: `emplace_back` forwards constructor arguments, so it takes no braces: `v.emplace_back({1, 2})` does not compile. `push_back` takes an object, so `v.push_back({1, 2})` is the braced form.
cards.code: v.emplace_back(1, 2);

cards.q:
With `using P = pair;`, sort `vector

v` by `.second` ascending, using a lambda.
cards.a: For `sort`, returning true means `a` comes first. That is the opposite reading from `priority_queue`, where `>` gives a min-heap.

cards.q: Why is this comparator a bug?
cards.a: A comparator must be a strict weak ordering, so `cmp(x, x)` must be false. `<=` breaks that, which makes the behaviour undefined, and `sort` can run out of bounds.

cards.q: Sort `vector<int> v` in descending order using a standard function object.
cards.a: `sort` takes an object, so write `greater<int>()` with parentheses. `priority_queue` takes a type, so there it is `greater<int>` without them.
cards.code: sort(v.begin(), v.end(), greater<int>());

cards.q: What does `stable_sort` guarantee that `sort` does not?
cards.a: Elements that compare equal keep their original relative order. That lets you sort by a secondary key first and by the primary key second.

cards.q: Rearrange `vector<int> v` in average O(n) so that `v[k]` holds the value it would have if `v` were sorted.
cards.a: Elements before `v[k]` are `<=` it and elements after are `>=` it, but neither side is sorted. The middle argument is an iterator, not the index `k`.
cards.code: nth_element(v.begin(), v.begin() + k, v.end());

cards.q: Put the `k` smallest elements of `vector<int> v` at the front in sorted order, in O(n log k).
