cards.a: The rest of the vector is left in unspecified order. If the front `k` need not be sorted, `nth_element` is cheaper.
cards.code: partial_sort(v.begin(), v.begin() + k, v.end());

cards.q: Turn `vector<int> v` into its sorted distinct values.
cards.a: `unique` only collapses adjacent duplicates, so sort first. It returns the new logical end and leaves the size alone, so `erase` must cut the tail.
cards.code:
sort(v.begin(), v.end());
v.erase(unique(v.begin(), v.end()), v.end());

cards.q: Sum `vector<int> v` into `long long total` so that large sums do not overflow.
cards.a: The type of the third argument is the type of the running sum, so a plain `0` adds in `int` and overflows. `accumulate` is in `<numeric>`.
cards.code: long long total = accumulate(v.begin(), v.end(), 0LL);

cards.q: Reverse `string s` in place using the STL.
cards.a: `reverse` takes an iterator range and returns `void`, so its result cannot be assigned. `string` has no `.reverse()` member.
cards.code: reverse(s.begin(), s.end());

cards.q: Set `int mx` to the largest value in non-empty `vector<int> v`.
cards.a: `max_element` returns an iterator, so dereference it with `*`. On an empty range it returns `end()`, and dereferencing that is undefined.
cards.code: int mx = *max_element(v.begin(), v.end());

cards.q: Set `int i` to the index of the smallest value in non-empty `vector<int> v`.
cards.a: Subtract `v.begin()` to turn the iterator into an index. On ties you get the first smallest element.
cards.code: int i = min_element(v.begin(), v.end()) - v.begin();

cards.q: Using `next_permutation`, set `int cnt` to the number of distinct orderings of `vector<int> v`.
cards.a: Sort first, because `next_permutation` returns false after the largest ordering, wherever you started. `do`-`while` counts the starting ordering too.

cards.q: `vector<int> parent(n)` needs `parent[i] == i` for every `i`. Set that with one STL call.
cards.a: `iota` is in `<numeric>` and writes consecutive values starting at the third argument. It overwrites existing elements, so the vector must already be sized.
cards.code: iota(parent.begin(), parent.end(), 0);

cards.q: What does this print?
cards.a: `16843009`, which is `0x01010101`. `memset` writes bytes, so only 0 and -1 give the expected `int` value. Use `fill` for anything else.

cards.q: Why does this not clear the whole array?
cards.a: `a` decays to a pointer, so `sizeof(a)` is the pointer size, not the array size. Use `n * sizeof(int)` or `fill(a, a + n, 0)`.

cards.q: What does this print?
cards.a: `cde`. The arguments are a start index and a length, not an end index.
cards.qcode:
string s = "abcdef";
cout << s.substr(2, 3);

cards.q: Set `string t` to the characters of `s` from index `l` to index `r`, both inclusive.
cards.a: The second argument is a length, so inclusive bounds need the `+ 1`.
cards.code: string t = s.substr(l, r - l + 1);

cards.q: Set `bool has` to whether `string s` contains `"ab"`.
cards.a: `string::find` returns an index, or `string::npos` if there is no match. It is not an iterator, so do not compare it with `s.end()`.
cards.code: bool has = s.find("ab") != string::npos;

cards.q: Convert `string s` to `int x`, then convert `x` back to `string t`.
cards.a: `stoi` throws `invalid_argument` when no digits can be read and `out_of_range` when the value does not fit. Use `stoll` for `long long`.
cards.code:
int x = stoi(s);
string t = to_string(x);

cards.q: What does `stoi("12abc")` return?
cards.a: 12. It parses the longest valid numeric prefix and ignores the rest, throwing only if there is no such prefix.

cards.q: Set `int d` to the numeric value of digit character `c`.
cards.a: Digit characters have consecutive codes, so subtracting `'0'` gives 0 to 9. `int d = c;` would give the character code, such as 48 for `'0'`.
cards.code: int d = c - '0';

cards.q: Set `char c` to the letter at 0-based position `i` of the lowercase alphabet.
cards.a: `'a' + i` is an `int`, and assigning it to `char` turns it back into a letter. `c - 'a'` is the reverse.
cards.code: char c = 'a' + i;

cards.q: What does this print?
cards.a: `98`. Arithmetic promotes `char` to `int`, so `cout` prints a number. `char('a' + 1)` prints `b`.
cards.qcode: cout << 'a' + 1;

cards.q: Read one whole line from standard input, spaces included, into a new `string line`.
cards.a: `cin >> s` stops at whitespace. `getline` reads up to the newline and discards it.
cards.code:
string line;
getline(cin, line);

cards.q: The input is `5` on one line and `hello` on the next. What does `line` hold?
cards.a: An empty string. `cin >> n` leaves the newline unread and `getline` stops there at once, so call `cin.ignore();` before it.

cards.q: Split `string line` on whitespace into `vector<string> words` using a `stringstream`.
cards.a: `ss >> word` skips any run of whitespace and fails at the end of the stream, which ends the loop. `stringstream` is in `<sstream>`.

cards.q: Store the product of `int a` and `int b` in `long long p` without overflow.
cards.a: `long long p = a * b;` still overflows, because `a * b` is computed in `int` before the conversion. Making the first operand `long long` widens the whole product.
cards.code: long long p = 1LL * a * b;

cards.q: Declare `int mid` halfway between `int lo` and `int hi`, safe from overflow.
cards.a: `(lo + hi) / 2` overflows when the sum passes `INT_MAX`. `hi - lo` stays in range for `0 <= lo <= hi`.
cards.code: int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;

cards.q: Summing 1e5 values of up to 1e9 each, which type does the total need?
cards.a: `long long`. The total can reach 1e14, while `int` stops near 2.1e9 and `long long` near 9.2e18.

cards.q: Set `long long best` to the largest `long long` value, using `numeric_limits`.
cards.a: `max()` is a function, so keep the parentheses. For `int`, the shorter `INT_MAX` from `<climits>` does the same job.
cards.code: long long best = numeric_limits<long long>::max();

cards.q: Why does `max(a, b)` not compile when `a` is `long long` and `b` is `int`?
cards.a: `max` takes two arguments of one deduced type `T`, and here the deduction conflicts. Write `max<long long>(a, b)` or cast `b`.

cards.q: Set `int best` to the smallest of `a`, `b` and `c` with a single call to `min`.
cards.a: The braces build an `initializer_list`, which has its own overload. `min(a, b, c)` is wrong, because its third parameter is a comparator.
cards.code: int best = min({a, b, c});

cards.q: What happens when this runs?
cards.a: `v.size()` is unsigned, so `v.size() - 1` wraps to a huge value and the loop reads out of bounds. Fix it with `int n = v.size();` and `i < n - 1`.

cards.q: Set `int ones` to the number of set bits in `int x`, using a compiler builtin.
cards.a: It takes an `unsigned int`, and `__builtin_popcountll` is the 64-bit form. Builtins are GCC and Clang extensions, not standard C++.
cards.code: int ones = __builtin_popcount(x);

cards.q: Set `int tz` to the number of trailing zero bits in nonzero `int x`, using a compiler builtin.
cards.a: The result is undefined for `x == 0`, so guard that case. `__builtin_ctzll` is the 64-bit form.
cards.code: int tz = __builtin_ctz(x);

cards.q: Declare `bitset<1000> b`, set bit 5, and store the number of set bits in `int ones`.
cards.a: The size is a compile-time constant. `b[i]` or `b.test(i)` reads a bit, and `b.to_string()` gives the binary text.

cards.q: With `deque<int> dq`, add `x` at the front, add `y` at the back, then remove the front element.
cards.a: Both ends are O(1), and `dq[i]` gives random access, which `queue` does not. Read the ends with `dq.front()` and `dq.back()`.

cards.q: Move the top of `stack<int> st` into `int x`, removing it from the stack.
cards.a: `pop()` returns `void`, so read `top()` first.
cards.code:
int x = st.top();
st.pop();

cards.q: Move the next element of `queue<int> q` into `int x`, removing it from the queue.
cards.a: `queue` uses `front()`, not `top()`; only `stack` and `priority_queue` have `top()`. Its `pop()` also returns `void`.
cards.code:
int x = q.front();
q.pop();

cards.q: Declare `cnt`, a fixed-size `array` of 26 `int` zeros.
cards.a: The empty braces zero it, while a local `array<int, 26> cnt;` holds garbage. Unlike a C array it compares with `==` and `<`, so it can be a `map` key.
cards.code: array<int, 26> cnt{};

cards.q: How does `<` compare two `pair<int, int>` values?
cards.a: By `first`, then by `second` when the firsts are equal. So `sort` needs no comparator for that order, and `priority_queue` puts the largest `first` on top.

cards.q: Declare `tuple<int, int, string> t` holding 1, 2 and `"a"`, then read its last field into `string s`.
cards.a: The index in `get<2>` is a template argument, so it must be a compile-time constant. A loop variable will not work.
cards.code:
tuple<int, int, string> t = {1, 2, "a"};
string s = get<2>(t);

cards.q: Unpack `pair<int, int> p` into new variables `a` and `b` in one line.
cards.a: Structured bindings need C++17. Plain `auto` copies, while `auto& [a, b] = p;` binds to the original.
cards.code: auto [a, b] = p;

cards.q: Add every value of `map<string, int> m` to `int total`, using structured bindings named `k` and `v` and no copies.
cards.a: Each element is a `pair<const string, int>`. `const auto&` avoids copying the string key on every step.
cards.code: for (const auto& [k, v] : m) total += v;

cards.q: What does this print?
cards.a: `1`. `x` is a copy, so the vector is unchanged. Write `for (int& x : v)` to modify elements.

cards.q: Add the length of every string in `vector<string> words` to `int total`, without copying any string.
cards.a: `auto w` copies each string. Use `const auto&` for anything larger than a small scalar that you only read.
cards.code: for (const auto& w : words) total += w.size();

cards.q: Given child lists `vector<vector<int>> adj`, define a recursive lambda `dfs` returning the size of the subtree at `u`, then store `dfs(0)` in `int total`.
cards.a: `auto dfs` does not compile, because the variable cannot appear in its own initialiser before its type is known. `function<int(int)>` names the type up front.

cards.q: What does storing a recursive lambda in `function<int(int)>` cost?
cards.a: Every call is an indirect call through type erasure that the compiler usually cannot inline, and constructing the `function` may allocate. That is fine for most interview code, but a named function is faster in hot recursion.

cards.q: Why must this lambda capture with `[&]`, not `[=]`?
cards.a: `[=]` copies `f` before `f` is initialised, which is undefined behaviour. `[&]` stores a reference, and `f` is ready by the time the lambda runs.

cards.q: Without `function`, define a recursive generic lambda `fact` that takes itself as `self`, then store `fact(fact, 5)` in `int ans`.
cards.a: The lambda receives itself as an argument, so there is no `function` overhead. The `-> int` is needed here, because the return type cannot be deduced through the recursive call.

cards.q: What are the two problems with this by-value `seen` in a recursive `dfs`?
cards.a: Each call copies the whole vector, which costs O(n) per call. Marks made by a deeper call are also lost when it returns, so declare `vector<int>& seen`.

cards.q: Write `struct PairHash` so that `unordered_map<pair<int, int>, int, PairHash> m` compiles, combining `hash<int>` of both fields with a multiplier of 31, then declare `m`.
cards.a: `std::hash` has no `pair` specialisation, so the map needs a hasher as its third template argument. `operator()` must be `const`. A `map<pair<int, int>, int>` needs no hasher at all, at O(log n) per access.

cards.q: Define `struct ListNode` with `int val`, `ListNode* next`, and a constructor `ListNode(int x)` that uses an initialiser list.
cards.a: Forgetting `next(nullptr)` leaves `next` uninitialised, so the first walk of the list can crash. Use `ListNode dummy(0);` for a stack node and `new ListNode(0)` for a heap node.

cards.q: Return the largest index `i` with `a[i] <= x` in a sorted array, or -1 if there is none.
cards.a: `mid` rounds down, so once `hi == lo + 1` the branch `lo = mid` makes no progress. `a = {1, 2}, x = 2` loops forever. Round up whenever a branch assigns `lo = mid`.
cards.code: int mid = lo + (hi - lo + 1) / 2;

cards.q: Return the first index whose value is at least `x`, or `a.size()` if there is none.
cards.a: With a half-open range the loop must stop at `lo == hi`, but `<=` keeps going and `hi = mid` then changes nothing. `a = {1, 3}, x = 2` loops forever. Use `lo < hi`, which also stops `a[mid]` reading past the end.
cards.code: while (lo < hi)

cards.q: Find the minimum of a non-empty rotated sorted array with distinct values.
cards.a: When `a[mid] <= a[hi]`, `mid` itself can be the minimum, and `hi = mid - 1` throws it away. `a = {3, 1, 2}` returns 3 instead of 1. Keep it with `hi = mid`.
cards.code: else hi = mid;

cards.q: Return the index of `x` in a rotated sorted array with distinct values, or -1.
cards.a: When `lo == mid` the left part is the single element `a[lo]`, but strict `<` sends the code to the branch for a sorted right part. `a = {3, 1}, x = 1` returns -1 instead of 1. Test `a[lo] <= a[mid]`.
cards.code: if (a[lo] <= a[mid])

cards.q: Return the integer square root of a non-negative int `n`: the largest `r` with `r * r <= n`.
cards.a: `mid * mid` is computed in `int` and overflows once `mid` passes 46340. `n = 2147483647` overflows on the first probe, and a plain build wraps to 0 and returns 1073741824 instead of 46340. Compare in 64 bits with `(long long)mid * mid <= n`.
cards.code: if ((long long)mid * mid <= n) lo = mid;

cards.q: Versions `1..n` turn bad at some point and stay bad. Return the first bad version for any int `n`.
cards.a: `lo + hi` overflows `int` when the sum passes `INT_MAX`. `n = 2147483647` overflows on the first step, and the negative `mid` keeps the loop from ever reaching the answer. Write `mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2`.
cards.code: int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;

cards.q: Find the smallest ship capacity that moves a non-empty package list, in order, within `days` days.
cards.a: Capacity must start at the heaviest package, because the feasibility check still loads a package that exceeds `cap`. `w = {5, 5}, days = 3` returns 1 instead of 5. Start `lo` at `*max_element(w.begin(), w.end())`.
cards.code: long long lo = *max_element(w.begin(), w.end()), hi = accumulate(w.begin(), w.end(), 0LL);

cards.q: Return the length of the longest substring with no repeated character.
cards.a: `last` still holds characters that already left the window, so `lo` can jump backwards. `s = "abba"` returns 3 instead of 2. Only move forward with `lo = max(lo, last[s[hi]] + 1)`.
cards.code: if (last.count(s[hi])) lo = max(lo, last[s[hi]] + 1);

cards.q: Given positive integers and `target > 0`, return the shortest subarray length with sum at least `target`, or 0.
cards.a: The length is recorded after the shrink, so it describes a window that may no longer meet the target. `a = {5}, target = 5` returns 0 instead of 1. Update `best` first, then remove `a[lo]`.
cards.code:
best = min(best, hi - lo + 1);
sum -= a[lo++];

cards.q: Return the length of the longest substring with at most `k` distinct characters.
cards.a: A key whose count reaches 0 stays in the map, so `cnt.size()` never drops. `s = "abac", k = 2` keeps shrinking and runs `lo` off the end of the string. Erase the key when its count hits 0.
cards.code: if (--cnt[s[lo]] == 0) cnt.erase(s[lo]);

cards.q: Return the length of the shortest window of `s` containing every character of `t` with multiplicity, or 0.
cards.a: After the decrement a required character is short only when `have < need`, so `<=` also fires for spare characters and ends the shrink early. `s = "xa", t = "a"` returns 2 instead of 1. Use strict `<`.
cards.code: if (--have[s[lo]] < need[s[lo]]) missing++;

cards.q: Return the maximum of every window of size `k`, with `1 <= k <= a.size()`.
cards.a: The window ending at `i` starts at `i - k + 1`, so index `i - k` is already out, yet `<` keeps it for one extra step. `a = {3, 1, 1}, k = 2` returns `{3, 3}` instead of `{3, 1}`. Pop when `dq.front() <= i - k`.
cards.code: if (dq.front() <= i - k) dq.pop_front();

cards.q: Return all unique triplets of values that sum to zero.
cards.a: Comparing with `a[i + 1]` skips the first copy of a value, so triplets that use that value twice are lost. `a = {-1, -1, 2}` returns nothing instead of `{-1, -1, 2}`. Skip only repeats of the previous anchor: `if (i > 0 && a[i] == a[i - 1]) continue;`.
cards.code: if (i > 0 && a[i] == a[i - 1]) continue;

cards.q: In a sorted array, keep each value at most twice in place and return the new length.
cards.a: `a[i - 2]` may already have been overwritten by the write pointer, so the check reads shifted data. `a = {1, 1, 1, 2, 2}` returns 3 instead of 4. Compare with what was kept: `if (w < 2 || a[i] != a[w - 2])`.

cards.q: Return every distinct subset of a list that may contain repeated values.
cards.a: Duplicates should only be skipped among siblings at one depth, but `i > 0` also blocks taking a second copy deeper down. `a = {1, 1}` returns `{}, {1}` and misses `{1, 1}`. Use `if (i > start && a[i] == a[i - 1]) continue;`.
cards.code: if (i > start && a[i] == a[i - 1]) continue;

cards.q: Count the subarrays whose sum equals `k`; values may be negative.
cards.a: The empty prefix is missing, so subarrays that start at index 0 are never counted. `a = {3}, k = 3` returns 0 instead of 1. Seed the map with sum 0 seen once.
cards.code: unordered_map<long long, int> seen{{0, 1}};

cards.q: Return the length of the longest subarray whose sum equals `k`; values may be negative.
cards.a: A repeated prefix sum overwrites its earliest index, and the longest subarray needs the earliest one. `a = {1, -1, 1}, k = 1` returns 1 instead of 3. Store only the first occurrence with `first.emplace(pre, i);`.
cards.code: first.emplace(pre, i);

cards.q: Count the subarrays of an integer array whose sum is divisible by `k > 0`.
cards.a: In C++ `%` keeps the sign of the left operand, so prefix -1 lands on index -1 instead of matching prefix 2. `a = {2, -3}, k = 3` reads `seen[-1]` and misses the subarray `{-3}`. Normalize with `pre = ((pre + x) % k + k) % k;`.
cards.code: pre = ((pre + x) % k + k) % k;

cards.q: For each element, return the next greater value to its right, or -1.
cards.a: `<=` pops on an equal value and records it as the answer. `a = {2, 2, 3}` returns `{2, 3, -1}` instead of `{3, 3, -1}`. Pop only on strict `<`.
cards.code: while (!st.empty() && a[st.back()] < a[i])

cards.q: Return the sum of the minimum of every contiguous subarray.
cards.a: Both passes stop at an equal value, so a subarray with a tied minimum belongs to no index. `a = {1, 1}` returns 2 instead of 3. Make the left pass pop on `>=` so each tie has exactly one owner.
cards.code: while (!st.empty() && a[st.back()] >= a[i]) st.pop_back();

cards.q: Return the largest rectangle area in a histogram.
cards.a: Bars still on the stack when the loop ends are never measured. `h = {1, 2, 3}` returns 0 instead of 4. Append a 0 bar before the loop so every bar gets popped.
cards.code: h.push_back(0);

cards.q: Compute how much rain water is trapped between the bars.
cards.a: After popping `bottom` the stack may be empty, so `st.back()` is undefined. `h = {1, 2}` reads an empty stack. Add `if (st.empty()) break;` right after the pop, since no left wall means no water.
cards.code: if (st.empty()) break;

cards.q: Remove the `n`-th node from the end of a list, with `1 <= n <= length`.
cards.a: When `n` equals the length the head is the target, `fast` ends up null and `fast->next` crashes. List `[1, 2]` with `n = 2` dereferences null. Return `head->next` when `fast` is null, or start both pointers from a dummy node.
cards.code: if (!fast) return head->next;

cards.q: Return the middle node of a list; for even length return the second middle.
cards.a: On an even-length list `fast` jumps to null, and the next loop test dereferences it. List `[1, 2]` crashes on the second check. Test both: `while (fast && fast->next)`.
cards.code: while (fast && fast->next)

cards.q: Return whether a singly linked list contains a cycle.
cards.a: Both pointers start equal, so the loop body never runs and the result only says the list has two nodes. List `[1, 2]` with no cycle returns true. Start `fast` one step ahead, at `head->next` when `head` is not null.
cards.code: ListNode* fast = head ? head->next : nullptr;

cards.q: Merge two sorted lists by relinking their nodes.
cards.a: Only the rest of `a` is attached, so whatever remains of `b` is dropped. `a = []`, `b = [1]` returns an empty list. Attach whichever of `a` and `b` is still non-null.
cards.code: tail->next = a ? a : b;

cards.q: Delete every node whose value equals `x`.
cards.a: The scan only inspects `cur->next`, so the head itself is never checked. List `[1, 2]` with `x = 1` stays `[1, 2]`. Start `cur` at a dummy node placed before the head and return `dummy.next`.

cards.q: Return the node where two lists meet, or null if they never meet.
cards.a: The pointers switch lists without ever stepping onto null, so disjoint lists never become equal. `a = [1]`, `b = [2]` loops forever. Let each pointer step onto null once before it switches lists.
cards.code:
p = p ? p->next : b;
q = q ? q->next : a;

cards.q: Implement an LRU cache with capacity `cap >= 1` and non-negative values. `get` returns -1 for a missing key.
cards.a: After `pop_back`, `items.back()` is a different entry, so the wrong key is erased and the evicted key keeps a dead iterator. With `cap = 2`, `put(1, 1), put(2, 2), put(3, 3), get(2)` returns -1 instead of 2. Erase from `pos` before `pop_back`.
cards.code:
pos.erase(items.back().first);
items.pop_back();

cards.q: Return the number of nodes on the shortest path from the root down to a leaf.
cards.a: A missing child returns depth 0, so `min` picks a path that ends at a node with one child, which is not a leaf. Root 1 with only left child 2 returns 1 instead of 2. When one child is null, recurse only into the other.
cards.code:
if (!root->left) return 1 + minDepth(root->right);
if (!root->right) return 1 + minDepth(root->left);

cards.q: Return whether some root-to-leaf path sums to `target`.
cards.a: Stopping at null accepts a path that ends at an inner node with one child. Root 1 with only left child 2 and `target = 1` returns true instead of false. Return false at null and compare the target at a real leaf.
cards.code:
if (!root) return false;
if (!root->left && !root->right) return target == root->val;

cards.q: Return the diameter of a binary tree in edges. The function is called once per tree on many trees.
cards.a: `best` is global and keeps the value from the previous tree. A 3-node chain followed by a single node returns 2 for the second tree instead of 0. Reset with `best = 0;` before calling `height`.
cards.code: best = 0;

cards.q: Return the values of a binary tree grouped by level, top to bottom.
cards.a: `q.size()` is read again on every pass while children are being pushed, so the level boundary moves. Root 1 with children 2 and 3 returns `{{1, 2}, {3}}` instead of `{{1}, {2, 3}}`. Freeze the size before the loop.
cards.code: for (int i = 0, sz = q.size(); i < sz; i++)

cards.q: Return whether a binary tree is a valid BST with distinct values in `[-2^31, 2^31 - 1]`.
cards.a: `n->val + 1` overflows at `INT_MAX`, so the lower bound of the right subtree wraps to `INT_MIN`. Root `INT_MAX` with right child 5 returns true instead of false. Use `long long` bounds and add `1LL`, because `n->val + 1` alone is still computed in `int`.
cards.code:
bool check(TreeNode* n, long long lo, long long hi)
return check(n->left, lo, n->val - 1LL) && check(n->right, n->val + 1LL, hi);

cards.q: Return whether a binary tree is a valid BST with values in `[-2^31, 2^31 - 1]`.
cards.a: The open bounds cannot express no limit in `int`, so a legal node equal to `INT_MAX` or `INT_MIN` is rejected. A single node 2147483647 returns false instead of true. Make the bounds `long long` and start from `LLONG_MIN` and `LLONG_MAX`.
cards.code:
bool check(TreeNode* n, long long lo, long long hi)
return check(root, LLONG_MIN, LLONG_MAX);

cards.q: Insert `x` into a BST through its root pointer.
cards.a: `root` is a copy of the caller's pointer, so the new node is assigned to a local and lost. Inserting 5 into an empty tree leaves the caller's root null. Take the pointer by reference: `TreeNode*& root`.
cards.code: void insert(TreeNode*& root, int x)

cards.q: Return the `k`-th smallest value in a BST, with `k` counted from 1.
cards.a: `k` is passed by value, so a visit in the left subtree does not reduce the caller's count. Root 2 with children 1 and 3 and `k = 1` returns 2 instead of 1. Share one counter with `int& k`.
cards.code: void walk(TreeNode* n, int& k, int& ans)

cards.q: Return the sum of all left leaves in a binary tree.
cards.a: `n->left` is dereferenced before anyone checks that it exists. A single node crashes. Guard with `n->left && ...`, and the `else` then handles the null child through the base case.
cards.code: if (n->left && !n->left->left && !n->left->right) sum += n->left->val;

cards.q: Return the BFS edge distance from `s` to every node, or -1 if a node is unreachable.
cards.a: Nodes are marked when popped, so a node already in the queue can be pushed again and get a larger distance. `g = {{1, 2}, {2}, {}}, s = 0` gives `dist[2] = 2` instead of 1. Mark at push: set `seen[s]` before the loop and `seen[v]` inside the `if`, and drop `seen[u] = 1`.
cards.code:
seen[s] = 1;
seen[v] = 1;

cards.q: Return the shortest distances from `s` in a graph with non-negative edge weights.
cards.a: `done[v]` is set on the first relaxation, which freezes a tentative distance before a cheaper path can improve it. Edges `0->1` weight 10, `0->2` weight 1, `2->1` weight 1 give `dist[1] = 10` instead of 2. Finalize at pop: `if (done[u]) continue; done[u] = 1;`, and remove the line in the relax.
cards.code:
if (done[u]) continue;
done[u] = 1;

cards.q: Count the nodes whose shortest distance from `s` is at most `limit`; weights are non-negative.
cards.a: A node improved twice has two heap entries, and the stale one is counted as well. Edges `0->1` weight 5, `0->2` weight 1, `2->1` weight 1 with `limit = 10` return 4 instead of 3. Skip stale entries right after the pop with `if (d > dist[u]) continue;`.
cards.code: if (d > dist[u]) continue;

cards.q: Return whether a directed graph contains a cycle.
cards.a: A node stays marked after its DFS finishes, so reaching it again by a second path looks like a back edge. The diamond `g = {{1, 2}, {3}, {3}, {}}` returns true instead of false. Use three states and set `state[u] = 2` when the node finishes; only state 1 means a cycle.

cards.q: Deep-copy a connected undirected graph, starting from one node.
cards.a: The clone is recorded only after its neighbours are visited, so a neighbour that points back recurses again. Two nodes linked to each other overflow the stack. Set `seen[n] = copy` before the loop.
cards.code:
seen[n] = copy;
for (Node* m : n->nbrs) copy->nbrs.push_back(cloneGraph(m, seen));

cards.q: Compute single-source shortest paths with a binary heap; weights are non-negative.
cards.a: `d` and `u` are bound to the heap's top slot, which `pop` and later pushes overwrite or free. Edges `0->1` weight 1 and `0->2` weight 5 gave `dist[2] = 6` instead of 5 in a plain build, because the first push changed `d`. Copy the entry: `auto [d, u] = pq.top();`.
cards.code: auto [d, u] = pq.top();

cards.q: Return a topological order of `n` nodes, or an empty vector if none exists.
cards.a: Nodes on a cycle never reach indegree 0, so the loop just stops and returns a partial order. `n = 3` with edges `1->2`, `2->1` returns `{0}` instead of `{}`. Return the order only if its size equals `n`.
cards.code: return (int)order.size() == n ? order : vector<int>{};

cards.q: Return whether `n` tasks can all finish given dependency edges `u -> v`.
cards.a: The `set` drops a repeated edge but `indeg` still counts it, so `v` never reaches 0. `n = 2` with the edge `0->1` listed twice returns false instead of true. Count only new edges: `if (g[u].insert(v).second) indeg[v]++;`.
cards.code: if (g[u].insert(v).second) indeg[v]++;

cards.q: Implement union-find, where `connected` reports whether two elements share a set.
cards.a: `unite` re-parents element `a` instead of its root, which cuts `a` away from its old set. `unite(0, 1)` then `unite(0, 2)` leaves `connected(1, 2)` false. Link the roots: `p[find(a)] = find(b);`.
cards.code: void unite(int a, int b) { p[find(a)] = find(b); }

cards.q: Count the connected components of `n` nodes given undirected edges.
cards.a: `p[i]` is only a parent, not necessarily the root, because compression happens only on nodes that `find` visited. `n = 4` with edges `(0, 1), (2, 3), (0, 2)` returns 2 instead of 1. Insert `find(i)` for every `i` instead.
cards.code:
set<int> roots;
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) roots.insert(find(i));

cards.q: Implement union-find that stays fast on `2 * 10^5` elements and as many queries.
cards.a: Parents are never shortened and unions are not balanced, so a chain costs O(n) per `find`. Uniting `(i, i + 1)` for `n = 200000` and then calling `find(0)` `n` times does about 4 * 10^10 steps and times out. Halve the path while walking: `x = p[x] = p[p[x]]`.
cards.code: while (p[x] != x) x = p[x] = p[p[x]];

cards.q: Return the cheapest price from `s` to `t` using at most `k + 1` flights, or -1.
cards.a: Relaxing in place lets one round chain several flights, so a round can use more than one hop. Flights `0->1` price 1, `1->2` price 1, `0->2` price 5 with `k = 0` return 2 instead of 5. Copy `dist` at the start of each round and read `prev[u]`.
cards.code:
vector<int> prev = dist;
if (prev[u] != INF && prev[u] + w < dist[v]) dist[v] = prev[u] + w;

cards.q: Return whether word `w` can be traced through adjacent grid cells without reusing a cell.
cards.a: The `#` mark is never undone, so a failed attempt keeps blocking cells that a later start needs. `g = {"aa", "bz"}, w = "aab"` returns false instead of true. Save the result of the recursive calls, restore `g[r][c] = w[i]`, then return.

cards.q: Count the ways to place `n` non-attacking queens on an `n` by `n` board.
cards.a: `r - c` is negative whenever `c > r`, so `d2` is indexed out of bounds. `n = 4` reads `d2[-1]` on the second column of the first row. Shift the index to `r - c + n`.

cards.q: Solve 0/1 knapsack with a rolling previous row.
cards.a: `prev` is a reference, so it is the same row as `cur` and an item can be taken twice. `w = {1}, v = {10}, cap = 2` returns 20 instead of 10. Take a real copy: `vector<int> prev = cur;`.
cards.code: vector<int> prev = cur;

cards.q: Solve 0/1 knapsack with a one-dimensional table.
cards.a: Going upward reads `dp[c - w[i]]` after this same item already updated it, which is the unbounded version. `w = {1}, v = {10}, cap = 2` returns 20 instead of 10. Iterate capacity downward.
cards.code: for (int c = cap; c >= w[i]; c--)

cards.q: Count the combinations of distinct coin values that sum to `amount`, where each coin may repeat and order does not matter.
cards.a: With amounts on the outside, each order of the same coins is counted separately. `coins = {1, 2}, amount = 3` returns 3 instead of 2. Loop over coins on the outside and amounts on the inside.

cards.q: Return the fewest coins that sum to `amount`, or -1 if it cannot be done.
cards.a: `dp[a - c]` can still be `INT_MAX`, and adding 1 overflows to a negative count that `min` keeps. `coins = {2}, amount = 3` returns a negative number instead of -1. Skip unreachable states with `dp[a - c] != INT_MAX`.
cards.code: if (c <= a && dp[a - c] != INT_MAX) dp[a] = min(dp[a], dp[a - c] + 1);

cards.q: Return the edit distance between two strings using insert, delete and replace.
cards.a: Only the first column is initialized, so turning an empty prefix into `b[0..j)` costs 0. `a = "", b = "ab"` returns 0 instead of 2. Add `for (int j = 1; j <= n; j++) dp[0][j] = j;`.
cards.code: for (int j = 1; j <= n; j++) dp[0][j] = j;

cards.q: Count the palindromic substrings of `s` with an interval table.
cards.a: `dp[i][j]` depends on `dp[i + 1][j - 1]`, which a top-down `i` has not filled yet and reads as 0. `s = "aba"` returns 3 instead of 4. Run `i` from `n - 1` down to 0.
cards.code: for (int i = n - 1; i >= 0; i--)

cards.q: Sink an island of `1` cells to `0` from a starting cell.
cards.a: The cell is read before the bounds are checked, and `||` evaluates left to right. `g = {"1"}` from `(0, 0)` reads `g[1]` on the first recursive call. Put all four bounds tests before `g[r][c]`.
cards.code:
if (r < 0 || c < 0 || r >= (int)g.size() || c >= (int)g[0].size() ||
    g[r][c] != '1') return;

cards.q: Return the `k`-th smallest element using a heap of at most `k` items, with `1 <= k <= a.size()`.
cards.a: A min-heap pops the smallest, so it keeps the `k` largest and returns the `k`-th largest. `a = {1, 2, 3}, k = 1` returns 3 instead of 1. Use a max-heap: `priority_queue<int> pq;`.
cards.code: priority_queue<int> pq;

cards.q: Merge `k` sorted lists with a heap of list heads.
cards.a: `priority_queue` pops the element that compares greatest, so `<` yields the largest head first. Lists `[1, 2]` and `[3]` return `[3, 1, 2]` instead of `[1, 2, 3]`. Flip it to `a->val > b->val` for a min-heap.
cards.code: return a->val > b->val;

cards.q: Sort players by score, highest first.
cards.a: `sort` requires a strict weak ordering, and `>=` claims two equal items each come first. 100 players with the same score is undefined behaviour and can read past the end of the array. Use strict `a.score > b.score`.
cards.code: return a.score > b.score;

cards.q: Return the fewest rooms needed for half-open meetings `[start, end)`.
cards.a: The comparator ignores `d`, so at equal times a start can run before an end. `{{2, 3}, {1, 2}}` returns 2 instead of 1. Use plain `sort(ev.begin(), ev.end());`, which puts -1 before +1 at the same time.
cards.code: sort(ev.begin(), ev.end());

cards.q: Remove all even values from `a` in place.
cards.a: `erase` invalidates `it` and shifts the next element into its slot, which `++it` then skips. `a = {2, 4}` leaves `{4}` instead of `{}`. Use `it = a.erase(it)` and advance only when nothing was erased.

cards.q: Return `start >= 1` followed by its repeated halvings, ending at 1.
cards.a: `push_back` inside a range-for invalidates its hidden iterators, and `end()` was fixed before the loop started. `start = 8` returns `{8, 4}` instead of `{8, 4, 2, 1}`. Loop by index and re-read `out.size()`.

cards.q: Sort the values and drop duplicates.
cards.a: `erase` with one iterator removes a single element, not the tail, and `unique` may return `end()`. `a = {1, 1, 1}` returns `{1, 1}` instead of `{1}`. Erase the range: `a.erase(last, a.end());`.
cards.code: a.erase(last, a.end());

cards.q: Return whether any two adjacent elements are equal.
cards.a: `a.size()` is unsigned, so `a.size() - 1` wraps to a huge value on an empty vector. `a = {}` reads out of bounds instead of returning false. Move the arithmetic to the safe side: `i + 1 < a.size()`.
cards.code: for (size_t i = 0; i + 1 < a.size(); i++)

cards.q: Return the leftmost index where the sum to its left equals the sum to its right, or -1.
cards.a: `accumulate` takes its working type from the initial value, so `0` sums in `int` even though `total` is `long long`. `a = {2000000000, 2000000000, 2000000000}` overflows and returns -1 instead of 1. Pass `0LL`.
cards.code: long long total = accumulate(a.begin(), a.end(), 0LL);

cards.q: Return whether `s` can be split into words from `dict`.
cards.a: The second argument of `substr` is a length, not an end index, so the piece is too long. `s = "abc"` with `dict = {"a", "b", "c"}` returns false instead of true. Write `s.substr(j, i - j)`.
cards.code: if (dp[j] && dict.count(s.substr(j, i - j))) { dp[i] = 1; break; }

cards.q: Return the longest palindromic substring of `s`.
cards.a: When the loop stops, `l` and `r` sit one step outside the palindrome, so its length is `r - l - 1` and it starts at `l + 1`. `s = "a"` gets `start = -1`, and `substr` throws `out_of_range`. Record `bestLen = r - l - 1` and `start = l + 1`.
cards.code: if (r - l - 1 > bestLen) { bestLen = r - l - 1; start = l + 1; }

cards.q: Return indices `{i, j}` with `i < j` and `a[i] + a[j] == target`, or `{}` if there are none.
cards.a: `pos[key]` inserts a default 0 on a miss, and a real partner at index 0 also reads as false. `a = {3, 4}, target = 7` returns `{}` instead of `{0, 1}`. Look up with `find` so a stored 0 and a missing key stay different.
cards.code:
auto it = pos.find(target - a[i]);
if (it != pos.end()) return {it->second, i};

cards.q: Support prefix queries and a word count on a map-based trie.
cards.a: `t->kids[c]` inserts a null child on every failed lookup, and `countWords` later follows it. With only `"a"` stored, `hasPrefix(root, "b")` then `countWords(root)` crashes. Use `find` in `hasPrefix` so a query never changes the trie.

cards.q: Sum the integers on each line of text and return one total per line.
cards.a: Reading to the end sets the stream's fail and eof flags, and `str()` does not clear them. `lines = {"1 2", "3"}` returns `{3, 0}` instead of `{3, 3}`. Call `ss.clear();` for every line.
cards.code: ss.clear();

cards.q: Return the largest sum of non-adjacent elements from a list of non-negative values.
cards.a: The base case touches index 1, which does not exist for a single element. `a = {7}` reads `a[1]` and writes `dp[1]`. Add `if (n == 1) return a[0];`.
cards.code: if (n == 1) return a[0];

cards.q: Return whether two strings are at most one insert, delete or replace apart.
cards.a: `size()` is unsigned, so when `a` is shorter the difference wraps to a huge value instead of going negative. `a = "a", b = "ab"` returns false instead of true. Subtract the smaller size from the larger one.
cards.code: if (max(a.size(), b.size()) - min(a.size(), b.size()) > 1) return false;

cards.q: Find the first index with `a[i] >= x` in a sorted array.
cards.a: `x` larger than every element, where the answer is `a.size()` and `a[mid]` must not be read there; a run of equal values, where stopping at the first hit returns a middle copy; `lo + hi` overflowing on ranges near `INT_MAX`.

cards.q: Binary search on the answer for the smallest feasible value.
cards.a: A lower bound below a hard minimum, such as a capacity under the heaviest item, because the feasibility check may still pass; no feasible value at all, which needs a separate check; overflow in `mid` or in the running total inside the check.

cards.q: Search a rotated sorted array.
cards.a: Two elements left, where `lo == mid` requires `a[lo] <= a[mid]`; duplicates such as `{1, 0, 1, 1, 1}`, where `a[lo] == a[mid] == a[hi]` hides the sorted side and forces a linear shrink.

cards.q: Find all unique triplets that sum to zero.
cards.a: Anchor dedupe against `a[i + 1]`, which loses `{-1, -1, 2}`, so compare with `a[i - 1]`; all zeros such as `{0, 0, 0, 0}`, which must give one triplet; repeats on the inner pointers after a match; `int` overflow when values approach the limits.

cards.q: Sort an array of 0s, 1s and 2s in one pass with three pointers.
cards.a: A value swapped in from `hi` is unseen, so `i` must stay put; stopping at `i < hi`, which leaves the last element unchecked in `{1, 0}`; an unsigned `hi` wrapping below 0 on an all-2s array.

cards.q: Find the longest substring without repeated characters.
cards.a: `abba`, where a last-seen index behind the window moves the left edge backwards unless you take `max`; updating `best` only on a repeat, which misses a window that reaches the end, as in `abc`; characters outside `a-z` when counting in an array of 26.

cards.q: Find the minimum window of `s` containing all of `t`.
cards.a: Repeated characters in `t`, where `aa` needs two copies, so a set is not enough; no valid window, which must not return `INT_MAX` or a leftover substring; measuring the window after the shrink instead of before it.

cards.q: Find the longest subarray with sum at most `k` using a sliding window.
cards.a: Negative values, where adding an element can lower the sum, so shrinking is invalid and you need prefix sums; `k < 0` with non-negative values, where `while (sum > k)` runs `lo` past `hi` and off the array.

cards.q: Count subarrays with sum `k`.
cards.a: Subarrays starting at index 0, which need the map seeded with `{0: 1}`; negative values and zeros, which rule out a sliding window; `k = 0`, where inserting the current prefix before the lookup counts an empty subarray; prefix overflow in `int`.

cards.q: Count subarrays with sum divisible by `k`.
cards.a: Negative prefixes, because `%` keeps the sign in C++ and -1 must become `k - 1`; the seed for remainder 0; a prefix that is never reduced, which can overflow `int`.

cards.q: Find the next greater element in a circular array.
cards.a: One pass misses answers that wrap around, so scan `2n` positions with `i % n`; equal values, where `<=` treats a tie as greater; an all-equal array, which must give -1 everywhere.

cards.q: Find the largest rectangle in a histogram with a stack.
cards.a: Increasing heights, where bars stay on the stack unless a final 0 sentinel flushes them; an empty stack after a pop, where the width is `i`, not `i - top - 1`; area overflow in `int` for large heights.

cards.q: Remove the `n`-th node from the end of a list.
cards.a: `n` equal to the length, which removes the head and needs a dummy; a one-node list, where the result is null; looping until `fast` is null instead of `fast->next`, which leaves `slow` on the target rather than before it.

cards.q: Reverse a sublist between positions `m` and `n`.
cards.a: `m = 1`, where the head changes, so start from a dummy; not linking the old first node to the node after `n`, which cuts the list; `n` at the tail, where that next node is null.

cards.q: Find the node where a list's cycle begins.
cards.a: No cycle, so test both `fast` and `fast->next` before stepping; testing `slow == fast` before the first move, which is true at once; starting `fast` one step ahead, which breaks the reset-to-head distance argument.

cards.q: Validate a binary search tree.
cards.a: A deep node that breaks an ancestor's bound while passing its parent's check; node values equal to `INT_MIN` or `INT_MAX`, which need `long long` or null bounds; duplicates, which strict comparisons must reject.

cards.q: Find the maximum path sum in a binary tree.
cards.a: All-negative trees, where the answer is the largest node and not 0; clamping a child's gain at 0 while still counting the node itself; returning a forked path to the parent, which may extend only one side.

cards.q: Find the lowest common ancestor in a binary tree.
cards.a: One target being an ancestor of the other, which the recursion must return at once; a target missing from the tree, which the usual version still reports as found; repeated values, so compare pointers instead of values.

cards.q: Serialize and deserialize a binary tree.
cards.a: Missing null markers, which lose the shape; negative or multi-digit values, which break character-by-character parsing; a read index passed by value, which repeats tokens.

cards.q: Find a BFS shortest path in a grid.
cards.a: Marking cells at pop, which queues them repeatedly and can blow up time and memory; start equal to target, which must return 0; a blocked start or target; swapped `m` and `n` on non-square grids.

cards.q: Run Dijkstra's algorithm with a heap.
cards.a: Marking a node done when first relaxed instead of when popped; stale heap entries, which need `if (d > dist[u]) continue;` before expanding or counting; `int` distances overflowing on long paths; negative edges, which the algorithm cannot handle.

cards.q: Run a topological sort with Kahn's algorithm.
cards.a: A cycle, where the output is shorter than `n` and that must be checked; repeated edges when adjacency is a set but indegree counts every copy; nodes that appear in no edge, which are lost if the node list is built from the edges.

cards.q: Flood fill a region with a new color.
cards.a: New color equal to the old color, where the recolor no longer marks cells and the recursion never ends; reading `g[r][c]` before the bounds check; recursion depth on a large uniform grid.

cards.q: Implement union-find with a component count.
cards.a: Uniting two elements already in one set, which must not decrement the count; linking elements instead of their roots; reading `p[i]` instead of `find(i)` at the end; deep recursion in `find` without union by size.

cards.q: Solve 0/1 knapsack on a one-dimensional table.
cards.a: An upward capacity loop, which reuses an item; `dp` filled with 0 when the weight must be met exactly, which needs a negative sentinel with `dp[0] = 0`; value totals overflowing `int`.

cards.q: Find the fewest coins that make an amount.
cards.a: Unreachable states at `INT_MAX`, where `+ 1` overflows to a negative count; amount 0, which must return 0; coins larger than the amount, which give a negative index; greedy choice, which fails on `{1, 3, 4}` for amount 6.

cards.q: Find the longest increasing subsequence with binary search.
cards.a: Equal values, where `upper_bound` allows ties and strict increase needs `lower_bound`; reading `tails` as the subsequence, which it is not.

cards.q: Count the ways to decode a digit string with `1 = A` through `26 = Z`.
cards.a: A leading `0`, which gives 0 ways; `10` and `20`, where the 0 only works with the digit before it; `30` or `00`, which make the whole answer 0; `27`, which is only one way.

cards.q: Find the maximum product subarray.
cards.a: A negative value swaps the largest and smallest products, so track both; updating `lo` from the already updated `hi`; a 0, which resets the run; a single negative element, which is its own answer.

cards.q: Parse a signed integer from a string.
cards.a: `-2147483648`, which overflows if you build the positive value in `int`; overflow that must be caught before `res * 10`; a sign with no digits after it; leading spaces and a stop at the first non-digit.

cards.q: Reverse the digits of an integer.
cards.a: A reversed value above `INT_MAX`, such as from `1534236469`; `abs(INT_MIN)`, which overflows; negative values, where `%` gives a negative digit; trailing zeros, which must vanish.

cards.q: Split a string on a delimiter.
cards.a: `substr(pos, n)` takes a length, not an end index; `find` returning `npos` for the last token; consecutive or trailing delimiters, which produce empty tokens.

cards.q: Merge overlapping intervals.
cards.a: A contained interval such as `[1, 10], [2, 3]`, where the end must be the `max` of both; unsorted input; touching intervals `[1, 2], [2, 3]`, which need a decision on `<` or `<=`.

cards.q: Find the minimum number of meeting rooms.
cards.a: A meeting that ends exactly when another starts, where ends must sort before starts for half-open times; comparing a new meeting with the last one added instead of the earliest end; input not sorted by start in the heap version.

cards.q: Rotate an array right by `k` steps.
cards.a: `k >= n`, which needs `k %= n`; an empty array, where `k %= n` divides by zero.

cards.q: Compute `x` to the power `n` by squaring.
cards.a: `n = INT_MIN`, where `-n` overflows, so widen to `long long`; `n = 0`, which gives 1 even for `x = 0`; under a modulus, the product of two residues overflowing `int`.

cards.q: Print a matrix in spiral order.
cards.a: A single remaining row or column, which the backward passes visit twice without `top <= bot` and `left <= right` checks; non-square matrices; an empty matrix with `g[0].size()`.

cards.q: Implement an LRU cache.
cards.a: `put` on an existing key, which must update and refresh without evicting; popping the list before reading the key to erase from the map; `get`, which must also refresh recency; capacity 1.

cards.q: Implement a stack with constant-time minimum.
cards.a: Repeated minimums, so the min stack must push on `<=`, or popping one copy loses the others; `pop` or `top` on an empty stack; differences overflowing `int` in the single-stack trick.

cards.q: Find two indices that sum to a target with a hash map.
cards.a: An element paired with itself, so look up before inserting; repeated values such as `{3, 3}`; a stored index 0 read through `operator[]` as false.

cards.q: Sort with a custom comparator.
cards.a: `<=` or `>=`, which break strict weak ordering and make `sort` undefined; ties that need a secondary key, since `sort` is not stable; a comparator written as `a - b < 0`, which can overflow.

cards.q: Count set bits by shifting an integer.
cards.a: Negative input, where `>>` on a signed value keeps the sign, so `while (x)` never ends and you need `unsigned`; `1 << 31`, which is negative as an `int`; `1 << 40`, which is undefined and needs `1LL`.

cards.q: What does `v.push_back(x)` cost, worst case and amortised?
cards.a: Worst case O(n), when the buffer reallocates and moves every element. Amortised O(1), because capacity grows by a constant factor, so n pushes move only O(n) elements in total.

cards.q: A custom array grows by a fixed 1000 slots instead of doubling. What do n appends cost in total?
cards.a: O(n^2): it copies everything every 1000 appends, and those copies add up to about n^2 / 2000. Only geometric growth gives amortised O(1).

cards.q: What does `v.erase(v.begin())` cost, and what happens if you drain a vector this way?
cards.a: O(n) per call, because every later element shifts left. Draining costs O(n^2) in total. Use a `deque`, a read index, or pop from the back.

cards.q: You keep a `vector` in order using `lower_bound` plus `insert`. What do n insertions cost?
cards.a: O(n^2) in the worst case. The search is O(log n), but each `insert` shifts O(n) elements, and the shifting dominates.

cards.q: On a `deque`, what do `push_front`, `push_back`, `operator[]` and a middle `insert` cost?
cards.a: The end pushes and `operator[]` are O(1). A middle `insert` is O(n), shifting elements towards the nearer end.

cards.q: `list::insert` is O(1). So why does inserting at index `k` cost O(k)?
cards.a: Reaching position `k` means following `k` links, since a `list` has no random access. The O(1) applies only once you hold an iterator to that position.

cards.q: What do `insert`, `find`, `erase` and `lower_bound` cost on `map` and `set`?
cards.a: O(log n) comparisons each, because both are balanced BSTs. With long keys, multiply by the cost of one comparison.

cards.q: Why is `lower_bound(s.begin(), s.end(), x)` on a `set` slower than `s.lower_bound(x)`?
cards.a: The free function makes O(log n) comparisons but O(n) iterator steps, because `set` iterators are not random access. The member function walks the tree in O(log n).

cards.q: What are the average and worst-case costs of an `unordered_map` lookup?
cards.a: O(1) on average and O(n) in the worst case, when many keys share a bucket. So n inserts can reach O(n^2), and crafted keys make this easy because `std::hash<int>` is the identity in libstdc++ and libc++.

cards.q: When is `map` a better choice than `unordered_map`?
cards.a: When you need keys in order, nearest-key queries such as `lower_bound`, or a firm O(log n) worst case. For plain lookups, `unordered_map` is usually faster.

cards.q: What do `top`, `push` and `pop` cost on a `priority_queue`?
cards.a: `top` is O(1). `push` and `pop` are O(log n), because an element moves at most the height of the binary heap.

cards.q: Building a heap of n items: what do `make_heap` and n separate `push` calls cost?
cards.a: `make_heap` is O(n), while n pushes are O(n log n) in the worst case. Bottom-up building sifts each node down at most its height, and most nodes sit near the leaves, so the heights sum to O(n).

cards.q: Compare the ways to get the k largest of n items.
cards.a: Full `sort` is O(n log n), a size-k min-heap or `partial_sort` is O(n log k), and `nth_element` is O(n) on average. `nth_element` leaves the k items unordered.

cards.q: What is the difference between amortised O(1) and average O(1)?
cards.a: Amortised bounds the total cost of any sequence of operations, with no randomness involved, as with `push_back`. Average assumes typical inputs or hashing, as with `unordered_map`, so a bad case can exceed it.

cards.q: Why is a monotonic stack O(n) despite a `while` inside a `for`?
cards.a: Each element is pushed once and popped at most once, so the `while` runs at most n times across the whole `for`. Count total pops, not pops per step.

cards.q: Why is a sliding window O(n) when `left` moves inside a loop over `right`?
cards.a: `left` only moves forward and stops at n at the latest, so its moves total at most n across the whole run. That gives O(n) as long as each add or remove is O(1).

cards.q: A queue is built from two stacks. What does `pop` cost, worst case and amortised?
cards.a: Worst case O(n), when the output stack is empty and everything moves across. Amortised O(1), because each element moves across at most once.

cards.q: What does union-find cost with path compression and union by size, and with neither?
cards.a: Together they give amortised inverse Ackermann time, effectively constant. With neither, trees can degrade into chains, and a find costs O(n).

cards.q: In T(n) = a T(n/b) + f(n), what do you compare to solve it?
cards.a: Compare f(n) with n^(log_b a), the total work at the leaves. If one is polynomially larger it dominates, and if they match you multiply by log n.

cards.q: Solve T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) and name an algorithm with this shape.
cards.a: O(n log n): log n levels, each doing O(n) work. Merge sort is the standard example.

cards.q: Solve T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1) and name an algorithm with this shape.
cards.a: O(log n): constant work on each of log n levels. Binary search is the standard example.

cards.q: Solve T(n) = T(n/2) + O(n). Where does this shape appear?
cards.a: O(n): the work is n + n/2 + n/4 + ..., which stays under 2n. Quickselect with good pivots has this shape.

cards.q: Solve T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(1). Where does this shape appear?
cards.a: O(n): the levels hold 1, 2, 4, ..., n calls, which sum to under 2n. Visiting every node of a balanced binary tree has this shape.

cards.q: Solve T(n) = T(n - 1) + O(n). Where does this shape appear?
cards.a: O(n^2): the work is the sum of 1 to n. Quicksort with worst-case pivots has this shape, and the master theorem does not apply because `n` shrinks by subtraction.

cards.q: Solve T(n) = 2T(n - 1) + O(1). Where does this shape appear?
cards.a: O(2^n): the number of calls doubles on each of n levels. Include-or-skip subset recursion has this shape.

cards.q: Is naive recursive Fibonacci O(2^n)?
cards.a: Yes as an upper bound, but the tight bound is about O(1.618^n). Memoising brings it down to O(n), because there are only n distinct states.

cards.q: Why can no comparison sort beat O(n log n) in the worst case?
cards.a: It must tell apart n! possible orders, and each comparison has two outcomes, so it needs at least log2(n!) comparisons. That quantity grows as n log n.

cards.q: Here `pat` has length `L`. What does this loop cost?
cards.a: O(nL) even when nothing matches, because each `substr` copies L characters before the compare starts. `s.compare(i, L, pat)` avoids the copy and stops at the first mismatch, though its worst case is still O(nL).
cards.qcode:
for (int i = 0; i + L <= n; i++)
    if (s.substr(i, L) == pat) cnt++;

cards.q: What do these two loops cost?
cards.a: The `+=` loop is O(n) in total, because appending is amortised O(1). The `b = b + 'x'` loop is O(n^2), because every step copies the whole string into a new one.
cards.qcode:
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) a += 'x';
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) b = b + 'x';

cards.q: A recursive binary search takes `vector<int> a` by value along with `lo` and `hi`. What does it cost?
cards.a: O(n log n) rather than O(log n), because each of the log n calls copies all n elements. Pass `const vector<int>&` instead.

cards.q: A backtracking function takes `vector<int> path` by value. What does that add?
cards.a: An O(n) copy at every node of the recursion tree, which can turn O(2^n) into O(n * 2^n). Pass by reference, and push before and pop after each recursive call.

cards.q: Keys are strings of length L. What does one lookup really cost in `unordered_map` and in `map`?
cards.a: `unordered_map` is O(L) on average, because hashing and the final compare both read the key. `map` is O(L log n) in the worst case, because each of O(log n) comparisons can scan the whole key.

cards.q: `sort` runs with a comparator that costs `c` per call. What is the total?
cards.a: O(c * n log n), because the comparator runs O(n log n) times. For strings of length L that means O(L * n log n), and a comparator taking its arguments by value also copies on every call.

cards.q: What does this loop cost?
cards.a: O(n^2), because `min_element` scans a whole prefix on every step. A running minimum gives the same result in O(n). Watch for `count`, `find` and `accumulate` inside loops too.
cards.qcode:
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
    best = max(best, v[i] - *min_element(v.begin(), v.begin() + i + 1));

cards.q: Over n strings of length L, what does `for (auto s : words)` add compared with `for (const auto& s : words)`?
cards.a: O(nL) in total, because `auto` copies every string even if the body only reads it. `const auto&` binds without copying.

cards.q: What do BFS and DFS cost with an adjacency list, and with an adjacency matrix?
cards.a: O(V + E) with a list, because each node and edge is handled a constant number of times. O(V^2) with a matrix, because each node scans a full row.

cards.q: What do BFS or DFS cost on an R by C map of cells with 4 neighbours each?
cards.a: O(R * C) time and memory. There are R * C nodes and at most 4 edges per node, so edges add only a constant factor.

cards.q: What changes in BFS if you mark a node visited when it is popped rather than when it is pushed?
cards.a: A node can sit in the queue once per incoming edge, so the queue can grow to O(E) rather than O(V). Mark on push.

cards.q: On a complete binary tree of n nodes, compare peak memory for BFS and DFS.
cards.a: BFS holds a whole level, up to about n/2 nodes, so O(n). DFS holds one root-to-leaf path, so O(log n).

cards.q: BFS runs over n dictionary words of length L, and each popped word tries all single-letter changes against a hash set. What does it cost?
cards.a: O(n * 26 * L^2): each word has 26L candidates, and building and hashing each candidate costs O(L). The second L is easy to miss.

cards.q: What does Dijkstra cost with a binary heap, and when does a plain O(V^2) array version win?
cards.a: O((V + E) log V) with a heap. On dense graphs, where E is near V^2, that becomes O(V^2 log V), so the array version wins.

cards.q: How many subsets do n items have, and what does it cost to output them all?
cards.a: 2^n subsets. Copying each takes up to O(n), so O(n * 2^n) in total, which is fine up to about n = 20.

cards.q: How many orderings do n distinct items have, and what does it cost to output them all?
cards.a: O(n * n!) to output them all, because each of the n factorial orderings has length n. That is about 3.6e6 orderings at n = 10, which is fine, and about 6e9 at n = 13, which is not.

cards.q: How many k-item combinations of n items exist, and what does it cost to output them all?
cards.a: C(n, k) combinations at O(k) each, so O(k * C(n, k)). The count peaks at k = n/2: C(20, 10) is about 1.8e5 and C(30, 15) is about 1.6e8.

cards.q: What is the standard upper bound for N-queens backtracking, and why?
cards.a: O(n!) complete placements, because each row must take a column not used so far. Counting partial placements adds only a factor of about e, and diagonal pruning keeps the real search far smaller.

cards.q: How do you compute the running time of a DP?
cards.a: Number of states times the cost of one transition. LIS has n states at O(n) each, so O(n^2).

cards.q: 0/1 knapsack is O(nW). Why is that called pseudo-polynomial?
cards.a: The cost scales with the numeric value of W, not with the digits needed to write it. W = 1e9 fits in one `int` yet makes the table hopeless.

cards.q: What does Held-Karp bitmask DP cost for n cities?
cards.a: 2^n * n states with O(n) transitions each, so O(2^n * n^2) time and O(2^n * n) memory. That is about 1.7e7 steps at n = 16 and about 4e8 at n = 20.

cards.q: Edit distance takes O(nm) time. How much memory does it need?
cards.a: O(min(n, m)) with two rows if you only want the distance. Reconstructing the edits from the table needs O(nm).

cards.q: A recursive DFS walks a chain of 1e6 nodes. What can go wrong?
cards.a: Stack overflow, because recursion uses O(depth) memory. A default stack is often about 8 MB, and 1e6 frames of tens of bytes exceed that. Use an explicit stack or BFS.

cards.q: What extra memory do merge sort and quicksort use?
cards.a: Merge sort uses O(n) for merging plus O(log n) stack. Quicksort uses O(log n) stack on average and O(n) in the worst case, unless it always recurses into the smaller side first.

cards.q: Roughly, what is log2 of 1e3, 1e5, 1e6, 1e9 and 1e18?
cards.a: About 10, 17, 20, 30 and 60. So n log n at n = 1e6 is about 2e7, and binary search over 1e18 takes about 60 steps.

cards.q: What does this nest cost?
cards.a: O(n), not O(n log n). The inner loop runs n, then n/2, then n/4 times, and that series stays under 2n.
cards.qcode:
for (int i = n; i > 0; i /= 2)
    for (int j = 0; j < i; j++) work();

cards.q: What does this nest cost?
cards.a: O(n log n): the inner loop runs about n/i times, and the sum of n/i is n times the harmonic series, about n ln n. Loops over multiples or divisors have this shape.
cards.qcode:
for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++)
    for (int j = i; j <= n; j += i) work();

cards.q: Roughly how many simple operations does C++ run per second, and what should you plan for?
cards.a: Roughly 1e8 to 1e9. Plan for about 1e8, which leaves room for constants and cache misses.

cards.q: `n` is up to 1e5. Which complexities fit?
cards.a: O(n log n) at about 1.7e6 fits easily, and O(n sqrt n) at about 3e7 usually fits. O(n^2) at 1e10 does not.

cards.q: `n` is up to 5000. What does that suggest?
cards.a: O(n^2) at 2.5e7 fits, so pairwise loops or a 2D DP are likely intended. O(n^2 log n) at about 3e8 is risky, and O(n^3) is out.

cards.q: `n` is up to 500. What does that suggest?
cards.a: O(n^3) at about 1.25e8 is probably the target. Think interval DP or Floyd-Warshall.

cards.q: `n` is up to 20. What does that suggest?
cards.a: Exponential work in n: O(n * 2^n) is about 2e7. Think bitmask DP or subset enumeration.

cards.q: `n` is up to 10. What does that suggest?
cards.a: Factorial work is allowed: 10! is about 3.6e6, so trying every ordering is likely fine.

cards.q: `n` is up to 1e9 or 1e18. What does that suggest?
cards.a: No linear loop and no array of size n. Aim for O(log n) with binary search, fast exponentiation or a formula. O(sqrt n) works at 1e9, about 3e4 steps, but not at 1e18, at 1e9 steps.

cards.q: A 1e4 by 1e4 `int` DP table: will it fit in memory?
cards.a: Usually not: 1e8 `int`s take 400 MB. If each row depends only on the previous one, keep two rows.

cards.q: `n` and `q` are each up to 2e5. Why does that rule out O(n) per query?
cards.a: The total is O(nq), which is 4e10. Multiply the limits, then aim for O(log n) per query, about 3.5e6 steps overall.

cards.q: What goes wrong here if `process` throws, and what is the RAII fix?
cards.a: The `delete[]` is skipped, so the array leaks. Hold it in a `vector<int>` or `unique_ptr<int[]>`, whose destructor frees it on every exit path.

cards.q: Why must a destructor not let an exception escape?
cards.a: Destructors run during stack unwinding, and a second exception in flight calls `std::terminate`. Destructors are also `noexcept` by default since C++11, so an escaping exception terminates anyway.

cards.q: What is wrong with returning this pointer?
cards.a: `x` is destroyed when the function returns, so the pointer dangles and using it is undefined behaviour. Return the value itself, or a smart pointer that owns heap memory.

cards.q: How does `new` differ from `malloc`?
cards.a: `new` allocates and runs the constructor, and `delete` runs the destructor before freeing. `malloc` returns raw bytes, and `free` runs no destructor.

cards.q: What can a pointer do that a reference cannot?
cards.a: A pointer can be null, can be reseated to another object, and supports arithmetic. A reference must bind at initialisation and stays bound, so assigning to it writes through to the object.

cards.q: Why can a `const string&` bind to a temporary when a `string&` cannot?
cards.a: Binding a non-const reference to a temporary would let you modify an object about to vanish, so the language forbids it. A `const` reference may bind, and that extends the temporary's lifetime to match the reference.

cards.q: What is the difference between `const int* p` and `int* const p`?
cards.a: `const int* p` is a pointer to const: you can reseat `p` but not write through it. `int* const p` is a const pointer: you can write through it but not reseat it.

cards.q: Why does `mutable` exist if `const` member functions promise not to change the object?
cards.a: `const` promises logical constness. `mutable` exempts members that do not affect visible state, such as a cache or a mutex, which a `const` function may still need to change.

cards.q: What do the rules of three, five and zero each say?
cards.a: Rule of three: a class with a custom destructor or copy operation usually needs all three. Rule of five adds the two move operations. Rule of zero: let members such as `vector` and `unique_ptr` own resources so you write none.

cards.q: What happens when this class is copied?
cards.a: The implicit copy constructor copies the pointer, so both objects delete the same array, which is a double free. Define deep copy operations, or use `vector<int>` and write no special members.

cards.q: What does declaring a destructor do to a class's move operations?
cards.a: It stops the compiler generating the move constructor and move assignment. Copies are still generated, so code that looks like a move silently copies.

cards.q: What does `std::move` actually do at runtime?
cards.a: Nothing. It is a cast to an rvalue reference, and real moving happens only if overload resolution then picks a move constructor or move assignment.

cards.q: What can you safely do with a moved-from `std::string`?
cards.a: Destroy it or assign a new value to it. It is in a valid but unspecified state, so do not rely on its contents.

cards.q: Why does this call copy instead of move?
cards.a: `move(s)` yields a `const string&&`, which cannot bind to the move constructor's `string&&`. It binds to the copy constructor's `const string&` instead.

cards.q: Inside `void f(string&& s)`, is the expression `s` an lvalue or an rvalue?
cards.a: An lvalue, because it has a name. The type says what it can bind to, not its value category, so moving from it still needs `std::move(s)`.

cards.q: Why is `return move(local);` usually worse than `return local;`?
cards.a: It blocks named return value optimisation, which can build the result in place with no move at all. A plain `return local;` gets NRVO or, failing that, an implicit move.

cards.q: When is `T&&` a forwarding reference rather than an rvalue reference?
cards.a: When `T` is deduced for that very parameter, as in `template <class T> void f(T&&)`, and likewise for `auto&&`. `string&&` and `vector<T>&&` are plain rvalue references.

cards.q: What does `std::forward<T>` do that `std::move` does not?
cards.a: It casts to an rvalue only if the caller passed an rvalue, which preserves the argument's value category. `std::move` casts unconditionally.

cards.q: What did C++17 change about copy elision?
cards.a: Initialising from a prvalue now constructs directly in the target, so `T x = T();` and `return T();` involve no copy or move. The type does not even need an accessible copy or move constructor. NRVO of a named local stays optional.

cards.q: How does a virtual call work in a typical implementation?
cards.a: Each polymorphic object holds a hidden vptr to its class's vtable, an array of function pointers. The call loads the vptr, reads the slot for that function and jumps indirectly.

cards.q: Why does a virtual call inside a base constructor not reach the derived override?
cards.a: While the base constructor runs, the derived part does not exist yet, so the object's dynamic type is the base. The call dispatches to the base version.

cards.q: What mistake does the `override` keyword catch?
cards.a: A signature that does not match the base function, such as a missing `const`, which would otherwise silently declare a new function.

cards.q: What does `run` print?
cards.a: `B`. `f` is not virtual, so the call is resolved at compile time from the pointer's static type.

cards.q: What does `show(Derived{})` print?
cards.a: `Base`. Passing by value copies only the `Base` subobject, and that copy's dynamic type is `Base`. Take `const Base&` to keep polymorphism.

cards.q: Why must a polymorphic base class have a virtual destructor?
cards.a: Deleting a derived object through a base pointer with a non-virtual destructor is undefined behaviour. In practice the derived destructor is skipped, which leaks whatever it owns.

cards.q: Why does `shared_ptr<Base> p = make_shared<Derived>();` run `~Derived` even without a virtual destructor?
cards.a: The control block is created for `Derived` and remembers how to destroy it, whatever pointer type is later used. `unique_ptr<Base>` has no such record, so it needs the virtual destructor.

cards.q: Why is `unique_ptr` usually as cheap as a raw pointer?
cards.a: With the default deleter it is one pointer wide, with no reference count or control block. Single ownership is enforced at compile time by being move-only.

cards.q: What does a `shared_ptr` control block hold?
cards.a: The strong count, the weak count and the deleter, plus any custom allocator. It also holds either the object itself or a pointer to it.

cards.q: What goes wrong here?
cards.a: Each `shared_ptr` creates its own control block with its own count, so both delete `raw`, which is a double free. Copy the first `shared_ptr` to share ownership.

cards.q: Is `shared_ptr` thread-safe?
cards.a: Only the reference counts. Separate copies can be used on different threads, but the pointed-to object is unprotected, and one `shared_ptr` instance must not be written while another thread accesses it.

cards.q: Why prefer `make_shared` over `shared_ptr<T>(new T)`?
cards.a: It makes one allocation holding both the object and the control block instead of two. That is faster and keeps them together in cache.

cards.q: When does `make_shared` keep memory alive longer than you expect?
cards.a: The object and control block share one allocation. The destructor runs when the strong count reaches zero, but the memory stays until the last `weak_ptr` is gone too.

cards.q: How do two objects holding `shared_ptr`s to each other leak?
cards.a: Each keeps the other's count above zero, so neither destructor ever runs. Make the back reference a `weak_ptr`, which does not add to the strong count.

cards.q: Why must you call `lock` on a `weak_ptr` rather than check `expired` and then use the object?
cards.a: The object can die between the check and the use. `lock` atomically returns a `shared_ptr` that keeps it alive, or an empty one.

cards.q: Why must templates usually be defined in headers?
cards.a: The compiler generates code per instantiation, so it needs the full definition in every translation unit that uses the template.

cards.q: What does SFINAE let you do?
cards.a: If substituting a type into a template's signature fails, that overload is dropped rather than causing an error. `enable_if` uses this to switch overloads on or off by type traits.

cards.q: What does `inline` actually mean in modern C++?
cards.a: It allows identical definitions in several translation units, with the linker keeping one, which is why header-defined functions and, since C++17, variables use it. As an optimisation hint it is weak.

cards.q: Why might the compiler delete this null check?
cards.a: Dereferencing null is undefined behaviour, so after `*p` the compiler may assume `p` is not null. It can then remove the check as dead code.

cards.q: How does signed integer overflow differ from unsigned overflow?
cards.a: Unsigned arithmetic wraps modulo 2^N and is well defined. Signed overflow is undefined behaviour, so the compiler may assume it never happens, for example that `i + 1 > i` always holds.

cards.q: Why is reading a `float` through an `int*` undefined behaviour?
cards.a: Strict aliasing lets the compiler assume pointers to unrelated types never refer to the same object, so it can reorder or cache the accesses. Use `memcpy` to reinterpret the bytes.

cards.q: Why can code with undefined behaviour pass in debug builds and break in release builds?
cards.a: The standard places no requirement on such code, and optimisers transform programs assuming it never happens. Debug builds skip those transformations, so the bug stays hidden.

cards.q: What is the static initialisation order problem, and how do you avoid it?
cards.a: Globals in different translation units are initialised in an unspecified order, so one's constructor can use another before it is constructed. Wrap the global in a function-local static, which is built on first use.

cards.q: What goes wrong when the returned lambda is called?
cards.a: `x` is captured by reference and dies when `make` returns, so the lambda reads a dangling reference. Capture by value with `[=]` or `[x]`.

cards.q: In a member function, what does `[=]` capture when the lambda uses a data member?
cards.a: It captures `this`, not a copy of the member, so the lambda dangles if it outlives the object. C++17's `[*this]` copies the whole object.

cards.q: How do you move a `unique_ptr` into a lambda?
cards.a: Use an init-capture. The closure is then move-only, so it cannot be stored in a `std::function`.
cards.code:
auto p = make_unique<int>(1);
auto f = [q = move(p)] { return *q; };

cards.q: Why can creating a short `std::string` avoid heap allocation?
cards.a: Typical implementations store short strings in a buffer inside the object itself, which is the small string optimisation. The size limit depends on the implementation.

cards.q: Why can moving a `std::string` invalidate pointers into it when moving a `vector` does not?
cards.a: A short string lives inside the object, so a move must copy its characters into the target, and pointers into the source do not follow. A `vector` move hands over its heap buffer, so element pointers stay valid.

cards.q: Why does `vector` grow by a factor rather than by a fixed amount?
cards.a: Geometric growth makes the total copy work across n pushes O(n), so `push_back` is amortised O(1). A fixed increment recopies the whole array every few pushes, which totals O(n^2).

cards.q: Which `vector` operations invalidate iterators?
cards.a: Any reallocation invalidates all iterators, pointers and references. Without reallocation, `insert` and `erase` invalidate those at or after the position.

cards.q: What is the bug in this loop?
cards.a: `erase` invalidates `it`, so the `++it` that follows is undefined behaviour. Use `it = v.erase(it)` and advance only when nothing was erased, or use the erase-remove idiom.

cards.q: Why does `vector` copy elements on reallocation if their move constructor is not `noexcept`?
cards.a: `push_back` offers the strong guarantee. If a throwing move failed halfway, the old buffer would already be partly moved from and could not be restored, so `vector` copies instead when it can.

cards.q: What do the basic and strong exception guarantees promise?
cards.a: Basic: after a throw, nothing leaks and invariants hold, but state may have changed. Strong: the operation either succeeds or leaves state unchanged.

cards.q: Why catch exceptions by `const` reference rather than by value?
cards.a: Catching by value copies the exception and slices a derived type down to the catch type. A reference keeps the real type, so `what()` dispatches correctly.

cards.q: What is `sizeof(S)` on a typical 64-bit platform?
cards.a: 12. Three padding bytes after `a` align `b` to 4, and three tail bytes make the size a multiple of 4.

cards.q: Why can reordering struct members shrink it?
cards.a: Padding fills gaps forced by alignment, so sorting members from largest to smallest alignment leaves fewer gaps. With a 4-byte `int`, `{char, int, char}` takes 12 bytes and `{int, char, char}` takes 8.

cards.q: Why is `sizeof` of an empty class at least 1?
cards.a: Two distinct objects must have distinct addresses. As a base class, though, the empty base optimisation can make it take no space.

cards.q: What do threads of one process share, and what does each keep private?
cards.a: They share the address space (code, globals, heap) and open file descriptors. Each thread keeps its own stack, registers, program counter and thread-local storage.

cards.q: Why does one bad thread usually take down the whole process, while a crashing child process leaves its parent alive?
cards.a: Threads share an address space, so a wild write corrupts everyone, and a fatal signal such as SIGSEGV ends the whole process by default. A child has its own address space, so the parent is only notified and can restart it.

cards.q: Why might a browser run each site in its own process rather than its own thread?
cards.a: A process boundary gives crash isolation and lets the OS sandbox each site, so one compromised page cannot read another site's memory. The cost is more memory and slower communication through IPC.

cards.q: Why is a switch between threads of one process usually cheaper than a switch between processes?
cards.a: The address space stays the same, so page tables do not change and the TLB and caches stay useful. A process switch loads new page tables, which invalidates translations unless the TLB is tagged.

cards.q: Where does most of the cost of a context switch come from in practice?
cards.a: Mostly from the aftermath, not the register save. The incoming thread starts with cold CPU caches and, across processes, a cold TLB, so it runs slowly until they refill.

cards.q: What does a high count of voluntary context switches suggest, compared with a high count of involuntary ones?
cards.a: Voluntary switches mean threads are blocking, often on I/O or locks. Involuntary switches mean threads are being preempted, which points to more runnable threads than CPUs.

cards.q: What does virtual memory give you that raw physical addressing cannot?
cards.a: Isolation between processes, a private contiguous address space for each one, and the ability to use more memory than RAM by paging to disk. It also lets the kernel share physical pages between processes.

cards.q: Why can two processes hold the same pointer value yet read different data?
cards.a: Each process has its own page tables, so the same virtual address maps to a different physical frame. An address only means something relative to a page table.

cards.q: With 4 KB pages, how is a virtual address split during translation?
cards.a: The low 12 bits are the page offset, which passes through unchanged. The upper bits are the virtual page number, which the page table maps to a physical frame number.

cards.q: Why do 64-bit systems use multi-level page tables instead of one flat array?
