cards.a: A flat table needs an entry for every virtual page, used or not, which is far too large for a 64-bit space. Multi-level tables allocate lower levels only for regions in use, so sparse address spaces stay cheap.

cards.q: Why would paging be too slow without a TLB?
cards.a: Every load and store would first need a page table walk, which adds several extra memory accesses. The TLB caches recent translations, so most accesses skip the walk.

cards.q: Why must the TLB be flushed or tagged on a process switch?
cards.a: Its entries describe the old process's address space and would translate the new process's addresses wrongly. A flush makes the new process start cold, while ASID or PCID tags let entries from several processes coexist.

cards.q: Why can huge pages speed up a program with a large working set?
cards.a: Each TLB entry covers far more memory, such as 2 MB instead of 4 KB on x86-64, so the same number of entries reach more data and misses drop. The cost is wasted memory when a huge page is only partly used.

cards.q: Why is `munmap` in a heavily threaded process more expensive than it looks?
cards.a: Other CPUs running that process may still cache the old translation in their TLBs. The kernel must interrupt them to invalidate those entries, a TLB shootdown, and they stall while it happens.

cards.q: Is a page fault always an error?
cards.a: No. Most faults are routine work such as demand paging, copy-on-write and stack growth. It only becomes SIGSEGV when the address is unmapped or the access violates the page's permissions.

cards.q: What separates a minor page fault from a major one?
cards.a: A minor fault needs no disk I/O because the page is already in memory or can be zero-filled, so the kernel only fixes the mapping. A major fault must read from disk, which can be orders of magnitude slower.

cards.q: What happens after a page fault on a valid page that is not in RAM?
cards.a: The CPU traps to the kernel, which finds a free frame, evicting a page if needed, and reads the data from disk. It then updates the page table and re-runs the faulting instruction.

cards.q: Why can adding more processes to a busy machine make throughput collapse?
cards.a: When combined working sets exceed RAM, pages are evicted and faulted back in constantly. This is thrashing: the CPU sits waiting on disk instead of doing work.

cards.q: Why can `malloc` succeed and the process still be killed later for lack of memory?
cards.a: Linux overcommits by default, so `malloc` can reserve address space while frames are assigned only on first write. If RAM and swap run out at that point, the OOM killer picks a process to kill.

cards.q: Why is stack allocation faster than heap allocation?
cards.a: Stack allocation only moves the stack pointer. A heap allocator has to find a free block, update metadata, possibly take a lock, and sometimes ask the OS for more memory.

cards.q: Why does a stack overflow show up as a segfault rather than a clean error?
cards.a: Growing past the stack limit touches an unmapped guard region, and that access faults like any other invalid access. Deep recursion and large local arrays are the usual causes.

cards.q: Why does `malloc` usually not make a system call?
cards.a: The allocator keeps free lists of memory it already got from the OS through `brk` or `mmap`. It only calls into the kernel when those lists cannot satisfy a request.

cards.q: Why can a long-running server use far more memory than its live objects need?
cards.a: Heap fragmentation. Freed blocks are scattered between live ones, so whole pages cannot be returned to the OS and large requests cannot reuse the small gaps.

cards.q: Why must programs use system calls to reach hardware instead of touching it directly?
cards.a: User-mode code cannot run privileged instructions or reach kernel memory, because the CPU faults if it tries. A system call is a controlled entry point where the kernel checks arguments and permissions before acting.

cards.q: Is a system call the same as a context switch?
cards.a: No. The same thread keeps running and only the privilege mode changes. A context switch happens only if the kernel then schedules another thread, for example because the call blocks.

cards.q: What happens on the CPU when a program makes a system call?
cards.a: The C library puts the call number and arguments in registers and runs a trap instruction, `syscall` on x86-64. The CPU switches to kernel mode and jumps to a fixed kernel entry point, which does the work and returns to user mode.

cards.q: What goes wrong if a round-robin time slice is too short, and if it is too long?
cards.a: Too short and the CPU spends much of its time on context switches. Too long and it degrades toward first-come-first-served, so interactive tasks feel slow.

cards.q: Why do schedulers favour I/O-bound tasks over CPU-bound tasks?
cards.a: I/O-bound tasks run briefly and then block, so running them first costs little CPU and keeps the system responsive. CPU-bound tasks still get all the time left over.

cards.q: Why can a high-priority thread end up waiting on a medium-priority one?
cards.a: Priority inversion: a low-priority thread holds a lock the high-priority thread needs, and a medium-priority thread keeps preempting the lock holder. Priority inheritance fixes it by temporarily raising the holder's priority.

cards.q: What failure does preemptive scheduling prevent that cooperative scheduling allows?
cards.a: Under cooperative scheduling, a task that never yields, such as one stuck in a loop, hangs everything else. A preemptive OS uses a timer interrupt to take the CPU back.

cards.q: Why does Unix split process creation into `fork` and `exec`?
cards.a: The gap lets the child set up its environment with ordinary code, such as redirecting file descriptors or dropping privileges. `exec` then replaces the program while those settings stay in place.

cards.q: What does `fork` return?
cards.a: The child's PID in the parent, 0 in the child, and -1 in the parent on failure.

cards.q: How many times is `x` printed?
cards.a: Four. Each `fork` doubles the number of running processes, and all four reach the `puts`.

cards.q: Why is calling `fork` from a multi-threaded program risky?
cards.a: Only the calling thread exists in the child. A lock held by another thread at that moment stays locked forever, so the child should call only async-signal-safe functions until `exec`.

cards.q: What is the difference between a zombie process and an orphan process?
cards.a: A zombie has exited but its parent has not called `wait`, so only its exit record remains. An orphan is still running after its parent died, and init adopts it.

cards.q: Why is `fork` cheap even for a process using gigabytes of memory?
cards.a: The child gets its own page tables pointing at the same physical pages, marked read-only, so no page data is copied up front. This is copy-on-write.

cards.q: What happens when a process writes to a copy-on-write page?
cards.a: The write hits a read-only entry and faults. The kernel allocates a new frame, copies the page, and points the writer at the copy with write permission.

cards.q: What is a file descriptor, concretely?
cards.a: A small integer that indexes a per-process table. Each entry points to a kernel open file description, which holds the offset and flags and refers to the inode.

cards.q: What differs between opening a file twice and calling `dup` on a descriptor?
cards.a: Two `open` calls create two open file descriptions with independent offsets. `dup` gives a second descriptor to the same description, so the offset is shared, which is also what a child inherits across `fork`.

cards.q: How does a shell implement `ls > out.txt`?
cards.a: After `fork`, the child opens `out.txt`, uses `dup2` to put it on descriptor 1, and then calls `exec`. `ls` writes to stdout as usual without knowing it was redirected.

cards.q: Why can a process reading from a pipe hang after the writer has finished?
cards.a: A reader sees end of file only when every write end is closed. A forgotten copy of the write end, often one the reader inherited across `fork`, keeps the pipe open.

cards.q: Why should a service be stopped with SIGTERM before SIGKILL?
cards.a: SIGTERM can be handled, so the process can finish in-flight work, flush data and exit cleanly. SIGKILL cannot be caught, blocked or ignored, so the process gets no chance to clean up.

cards.q: Why is calling `printf` or `malloc` inside a signal handler unsafe?
cards.a: The signal can arrive while the thread is inside those same functions, holding their lock or with their data half updated. Re-entering can deadlock or corrupt state, so handlers should call only async-signal-safe functions or set a `volatile sig_atomic_t` flag.

cards.q: Which four conditions must all hold for a deadlock?
cards.a: Mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, and circular wait. Removing any one of them makes deadlock impossible.

cards.q: How do deadlock prevention, avoidance and detection differ?
cards.a: Prevention designs out a necessary condition, such as by using a global lock order. Avoidance checks each request and refuses any that could lead to an unsafe state. Detection lets deadlock happen, finds a cycle in the wait-for graph, and aborts a participant.

cards.q: What does an inode hold, and what is missing from it?
cards.a: It holds metadata such as size, owner, permissions, timestamps and link count, plus the locations of the data blocks. The file name is missing, because names live in directory entries.

cards.q: What happens to a hard link and to a symlink when the original name is deleted?
cards.a: A hard link is another directory entry for the same inode, so the data stays reachable. A symlink is a small file holding a path, so it dangles.

cards.q: Why can writes fail with "no space left on device" while `df` shows free blocks?
cards.a: The filesystem may have run out of inodes, often from millions of tiny files. Check with `df -i`.

cards.q: Why does deleting a large log file sometimes free no disk space?
cards.a: `rm` only removes the directory entry. If a process still has the file open, the inode and its blocks stay allocated until the last descriptor closes.

cards.q: Why does a database call `fsync` at commit when `write` already returned success?
cards.a: `write` only copies into the page cache and marks it dirty, and the kernel writes it back later. A crash in that window loses the data, so `fsync` blocks until it reaches stable storage.

cards.q: Why does a healthy Linux machine show almost no free memory?
cards.a: The kernel uses spare RAM as page cache for file data, because idle memory is wasted. That cache is reclaimed on demand, so "available" is the figure to watch, not "free".

cards.q: Why can the last `printf` output vanish when a program crashes?
cards.a: stdio buffers output in user space, by line on a terminal but in larger blocks on a file or pipe. If the process dies before a flush, the buffer never reaches the kernel.

cards.q: Why can `mmap` beat `read` for random access to a large file?
cards.a: Page cache pages are mapped straight into the address space, so there is no copy into a user buffer and no system call per access. After the first fault, each access is an ordinary memory load.

cards.q: What is the difference between `MAP_SHARED` and `MAP_PRIVATE`?
cards.a: With `MAP_SHARED`, writes go to the underlying file and other mappings see them. With `MAP_PRIVATE`, the first write to a page makes a private copy, so the file never changes.

cards.q: Why can reading a memory-mapped file crash with SIGBUS?
cards.a: Another process may have truncated the file, so the mapped page no longer has data behind it. With `read` this would be a short read, but a load instruction has no return value to report it.

cards.q: What is the difference between a data race and a race condition?
cards.a: A data race is unsynchronised access to the same memory by two threads, at least one writing, and in C++ it is undefined behaviour. A race condition is a logic bug where the outcome depends on timing, and it can exist even when every access is locked.

cards.q: Why can two threads each running `counter++` on a shared int lose updates?
cards.a: `counter++` is a read, an add and a write. If both threads read the same value, one increment overwrites the other.

cards.q: Why is `if (!m.count(k)) m[k] = v;` a bug even if each map call is individually thread-safe?
cards.a: Another thread can insert between the check and the write. Thread-safe calls do not compose, so the pair needs one lock or a single atomic insert-if-absent operation.

cards.q: A mutex gives mutual exclusion. What second guarantee does it give?
cards.a: Visibility. An unlock synchronises with the next lock of that mutex, so the next holder sees every write made inside the critical section.

cards.q: When is a spinlock better than a blocking mutex?
cards.a: When the lock is held for less time than a sleep and wake would cost, and the waiter runs on a different core from the holder. On a single core, spinning wastes the time the holder needs to finish.

cards.q: Why does locking an uncontended mutex on Linux usually avoid a system call?
cards.a: glibc mutexes are built on futexes, where the lock state is an atomic word in user space. Taking a free lock is one atomic compare-and-swap, and the kernel is involved only when a thread must sleep or be woken.

cards.q: What happens if a thread locks a `std::mutex` it already holds?
cards.a: Undefined behaviour, and in practice it often deadlocks. `std::recursive_mutex` permits re-locking by the same thread.

cards.q: What is the bug in this blocking pop?
cards.a: The `if` must be a `while`, or `wait` must take a predicate. `wait` can return spuriously, or another consumer can empty the queue first, so `q.front()` may run on an empty queue.

cards.q: Why does a condition variable need a mutex?
cards.a: The condition lives in shared state, so checking it needs a lock. `wait` atomically releases the mutex and sleeps, so no notify can slip between the check and the sleep.

cards.q: Why must the waited-on flag be set while holding the mutex, even if the flag is `atomic<bool>`?
cards.a: Without the lock, the update and notify can land after the waiter checked the flag but before it sleeps. The notify finds nobody waiting, so the waiter sleeps forever, which is a lost wakeup.

cards.q: When is `notify_one` wrong where `notify_all` is right?
cards.a: When waiters wait for different conditions, or when one state change can unblock several of them. `notify_one` may then wake a thread that cannot proceed while a runnable one stays asleep.

cards.q: How does a binary semaphore differ from a mutex?
cards.a: A semaphore is a counter with no owner, so one thread can wait and a different thread can signal, which suits signalling between threads. A mutex has an owner: the thread that locked it must unlock it.

cards.q: Why can a read-write lock be slower than a plain mutex for short reads?
cards.a: Every reader still writes the shared reader count, so that cache line bounces between cores. The gain only appears when reads dominate and their sections are long enough to overlap.

cards.q: What starvation risk comes with a read-write lock?
cards.a: If readers are always preferred, a steady stream of them keeps the reader count above zero and writers wait forever. Writer-preferring locks block new readers once a writer queues, which shifts the risk to readers.

cards.q: How can this code deadlock?
cards.a: `transfer(x, y, n)` and `transfer(y, x, n)` running at once lock the same two mutexes in opposite orders, so each can hold one and wait for the other. Lock in a global order such as account id, or take both with one `scoped_lock`.

cards.q: How does `std::scoped_lock` take several mutexes safely when callers disagree on the order?
cards.a: It uses a deadlock-avoidance algorithm, typically try-and-back-off. It locks one mutex and tries the rest, and on failure releases what it holds and retries, so it never blocks while holding the others.

cards.q: Why is calling an unknown callback while holding a lock dangerous?
cards.a: The callback may take other locks or re-enter your code, which creates a lock order you cannot see or control. Copy what it needs, release the lock, and then call it.

cards.q: How does livelock differ from deadlock?
cards.a: In deadlock, threads are blocked and idle. In livelock, they keep running and reacting to each other, such as backing off and retrying in step, but make no progress. Randomised backoff breaks the symmetry.

cards.q: On an `atomic<int> a`, why is `++a` safe while `a = a + 1` is not?
cards.a: `++a` is one indivisible read-modify-write. `a = a + 1` is an atomic load followed by a separate atomic store, so another thread's update between them is lost.

cards.q: Why can an atomic replace a mutex for a counter but not for keeping two fields consistent?
cards.a: An atomic makes operations on one location indivisible. An invariant across two locations needs both updates to appear together, which takes a lock or packing both into one atomic word.

cards.q: Why does this loop never reload `old` itself?
cards.a: On failure, `compare_exchange_weak` writes the current value into `old`, so the next pass recomputes from fresh data. This read-compute-swap retry is the standard lock-free update.

cards.q: Why can a successful compare-and-swap still be wrong in a lock-free stack?
cards.a: The head may have changed from node A to B and back to A, so the swap succeeds even though A's next pointer is stale. This is the ABA problem, and tagged pointers or hazard pointers address it.

cards.q: Is `volatile` enough to share a flag between C++ threads?
cards.a: No. It only stops the compiler from removing or merging accesses, and gives no atomicity or ordering, so it is still a data race. Use `std::atomic`.

cards.q: Why can another thread observe your writes in a different order from the one in your code?
cards.a: Compilers and CPUs reorder memory operations when single-threaded behaviour is unchanged, and store buffers delay when writes become visible. Only synchronisation creates ordering between threads.

cards.q: What does a release store paired with an acquire load guarantee?
cards.a: If the acquire load reads the value from the release store, every write made before that store is visible to the reader after the load. That is how one thread safely publishes data to another.

cards.q: When is `memory_order_relaxed` safe?
cards.a: When only the atomic's own value matters and no other data depends on it, such as a statistics counter. It keeps atomicity but gives no ordering, so it cannot publish data.

cards.q: Why is `seq_cst` the default for `std::atomic`, and why might you avoid it?
cards.a: It gives a single total order of those operations that all threads agree on, which is the easiest model to reason about. It can need extra fences, so hot paths may use acquire and release instead.

cards.q: Why can two threads updating two different variables run slower than one thread updating both?
cards.a: If the variables share a cache line, each write invalidates the line in the other core's cache, so it bounces between them. This is false sharing, and padding or `alignas(64)` puts each variable on its own line.

cards.q: Why use a thread pool rather than a new thread per task?
cards.a: Thread creation has real cost, and unbounded threads waste memory and time on context switches. A pool reuses a fixed set of threads and bounds concurrency, with excess work waiting in a queue.

cards.q: How should thread pool size differ for CPU-bound and I/O-bound work?
cards.a: CPU-bound work needs about one thread per core, because more only adds switching. I/O-bound work can use more, roughly cores times (1 + wait time / compute time).

cards.q: How can a fixed-size thread pool deadlock with no locks at all?
cards.a: Tasks submit subtasks to the same pool and block waiting for them. Once every worker is waiting, nobody is left to run the subtasks.

cards.q: Why should a producer-consumer queue be bounded?
cards.a: With no bound, producers that outpace consumers grow the queue until memory runs out. A bound blocks or rejects producers, which applies backpressure.

cards.q: Why does a bounded blocking queue commonly use two condition variables?
cards.a: Producers wait for "not full" and consumers wait for "not empty". With a single one, `notify_one` can wake a thread of the wrong kind, so you would need `notify_all`.

cards.q: What is the difference between concurrency and parallelism?
cards.a: Concurrency is structuring tasks so they overlap in time, which works even on one core. Parallelism is running them at the same instant on multiple cores.

cards.q: How can a single-threaded server handle thousands of connections?
cards.a: Connections mostly wait on the network. An event loop uses a readiness API such as `epoll` and runs only the handlers that can progress, so waiting connections cost no thread.

cards.q: What happens to an async event loop if one handler does a long CPU computation?
cards.a: Every other task stalls, because they all share that thread. Long CPU work belongs on a worker pool so the loop stays responsive.

cards.q: Why is this lazy initialisation broken?
cards.a: The first read of `inst` takes no lock, so it is a data race with the write. A thread can see a non-null pointer before the object's fields are visible, so `inst` must be `atomic` with acquire and release ordering.

cards.q: What is the simplest thread-safe lazy singleton in C++11 and later?
cards.a: A function-local static. The language guarantees it is initialised exactly once, and other threads wait until that finishes.

cards.q: What happens if a `std::thread` object is destroyed while still joinable?
cards.a: `std::terminate` is called. You must `join` or `detach` on every path, including when an exception unwinds.

cards.q: Why does passing a local to a thread function that takes `int&` need `std::ref`?
cards.a: `std::thread` copies its arguments into storage owned by the new thread, so a plain `x` cannot bind to `int&` and the call fails to compile. `std::ref(x)` passes a reference wrapper, and the local must outlive the thread.

cards.q: How does `lock_guard` differ from `unique_lock`?
cards.a: `lock_guard` locks in its constructor and unlocks in its destructor, nothing more. `unique_lock` adds deferred locking, manual unlock and relock, and moving, which is why `condition_variable::wait` requires it.

cards.q: What is the bug here?
cards.a: `lock_guard<mutex>{m};` creates an unnamed temporary that unlocks at the end of that statement, so the increment runs unprotected. Give the guard a name.

cards.q: Which C++17 types give you a read-write lock?
cards.a: `std::shared_mutex`, with `std::shared_lock` for readers and `std::unique_lock` for writers.

cards.q: Why can `async(launch::async, f);` with the result discarded behave as if it ran synchronously?
cards.a: The returned future's destructor blocks until the task finishes, and a discarded future is destroyed at the end of the statement. Keep the future in a variable to let the work overlap.

cards.q: What does TCP give you over UDP, and what does it cost?
cards.a: TCP gives reliable, in-order bytes plus flow and congestion control. The cost is a connection handshake, larger headers, and delays from retransmission and ordering.

cards.q: Why do live voice and video often use UDP instead of TCP?
cards.a: A late packet is useless for live media, so retransmitting it wastes time. TCP's in-order delivery would stall everything behind a lost packet, while UDP lets the app skip it and move on.

cards.q: Why can one `recv` on a TCP socket return half a message or two messages at once?
cards.a: TCP is a byte stream with no message boundaries, so bytes arrive however the network and buffers split them. Protocols must frame messages themselves, with a length prefix or a delimiter.

cards.q: What are the three steps of the TCP handshake?
cards.a: The client sends a SYN with its initial sequence number. The server replies with a SYN-ACK carrying its own number and acknowledging the client's. The client sends an ACK, and data can flow.

cards.q: Why does TCP need three handshake messages rather than two?
cards.a: Each side must have its initial sequence number acknowledged, and the server's number is only confirmed by the third message. It also stops a delayed old SYN from opening a connection, because the client never confirms it.

cards.q: Why does closing a TCP connection usually take four segments when opening takes three?
cards.a: Each direction closes on its own. The peer ACKs a FIN at once but may still have data to send, so its own FIN can come much later.

cards.q: How does a TCP close with FIN differ from one with RST?
cards.a: FIN is an orderly close: everything sent so far is delivered first. RST aborts the connection: buffered data is discarded and the peer sees a connection reset error.

cards.q: What is the difference between flow control and congestion control?
cards.a: Flow control protects the receiver, which advertises how much it can buffer. Congestion control protects the network, with the sender estimating how much the path can carry.

cards.q: How does a TCP sender's congestion window grow in slow start, and what happens next?
cards.a: It roughly doubles every round trip until it reaches a threshold or sees loss. Congestion avoidance then grows it by about one segment per round trip.

cards.q: Why does classic TCP grow its window slowly but cut it sharply on loss?
cards.a: It treats loss as a sign of congestion. Additive increase probes for spare capacity and multiplicative decrease backs off fast, which makes competing flows converge toward a fair share.

cards.q: Why can a fast long-distance link still give low TCP throughput?
cards.a: A sender can have only one window of unacknowledged data per round trip, so throughput is at most window divided by RTT. The window must reach bandwidth times RTT to fill the link.

cards.q: Why does TIME_WAIT exist?
cards.a: The side that closed first waits for twice the maximum segment lifetime. That lets it resend the final ACK if the peer's FIN is retransmitted, and lets stray segments expire so they cannot land in a new connection on the same ports.

cards.q: Why can a proxy making many short backend connections run out of ports?
cards.a: Each connection to one backend address needs a distinct local port, and the side that closes first keeps that port in TIME_WAIT after closing. Short connections can exhaust the ephemeral range, so the fix is pooling and reusing connections.

cards.q: Why do servers set `SO_REUSEADDR` before `bind`?
cards.a: Without it, a restarted server can fail with "address already in use" while old connections on that port sit in TIME_WAIT.

cards.q: What does a growing pile of sockets in CLOSE_WAIT point to?
cards.a: The peer has closed but your application has not called `close`, so it is usually a leak in your code. Unlike TIME_WAIT, it does not clear on a timer.

cards.q: What does HTTP/2 multiplexing solve that HTTP/1.1 keep-alive does not?
cards.a: An HTTP/1.1 connection carries one response at a time in order, so a slow response holds up those behind it and browsers open several connections. HTTP/2 interleaves many concurrent streams on one connection.

cards.q: Why did HTTP/2 not fully remove head-of-line blocking?
cards.a: It removed blocking at the HTTP layer, but all streams still share one TCP connection. TCP delivers bytes in order, so one lost packet stalls every stream until it is retransmitted.

cards.q: Why is HTTP/3 built on QUIC over UDP rather than on an improved TCP?
cards.a: TCP lives in kernels and is inspected by middleboxes, so changing it is very slow. QUIC runs over UDP, usually in user space, gives each stream independent loss recovery, and builds in TLS 1.3.

cards.q: Why can a QUIC connection survive a phone moving from Wi-Fi to cellular when a TCP connection cannot?
cards.a: TCP identifies a connection by its IP and port 4-tuple, so a new IP address breaks it. QUIC identifies it with a connection ID, so it can continue from the new address.

cards.q: Why does TLS use asymmetric crypto only in the handshake?
cards.a: Asymmetric crypto is far slower, so it is used to authenticate the server and agree on a shared secret. Bulk data then uses fast symmetric encryption with keys derived from that secret.

cards.q: What happens in a TLS 1.3 handshake?
cards.a: The client sends its supported ciphers and a key share. The server replies with its key share, its certificate and a signature proving it owns the private key. Both sides derive session keys, so encrypted data can flow after one round trip.

cards.q: How does a client decide to trust a server's certificate?
cards.a: It verifies the signature chain up to a root CA in its trust store. It then checks that the hostname matches and that the certificate has not expired.

cards.q: Why can a stolen server private key not decrypt previously recorded TLS 1.3 traffic?
cards.a: Session keys come from ephemeral Diffie-Hellman keys that are discarded after the handshake. The long-term key only signs the handshake, so it cannot recover them. This property is forward secrecy.

cards.q: How does `www.example.com` get resolved with empty caches?
cards.a: Your machine asks a recursive resolver. The resolver asks a root server, then the `.com` TLD server, then the domain's authoritative server, each pointing it to the next. It returns the answer and caches it for the record's TTL.

cards.q: What is the trade-off in choosing a DNS TTL?
cards.a: A low TTL lets changes and failovers spread quickly but causes more lookups, adding latency and load. A high TTL saves lookups but leaves stale records in caches for longer after a change.

cards.q: Why does DNS normally use UDP rather than TCP?
cards.a: A query and reply usually fit in one packet each, so a TCP handshake would add a round trip for little benefit. Clients retry on timeout and fall back to TCP when a response is truncated.

cards.q: How does a CDN send a user to a nearby edge server?
cards.a: Either its DNS returns the address of a nearby edge, or anycast announces the same IP from many sites and BGP routing picks a close one.

cards.q: Why do sites put a content hash in static file names?
cards.a: A changed file gets a new URL, so assets can be cached with a very long TTL and never need a purge. Browsers and CDNs cannot serve a stale copy under the new name.

cards.q: How does an L4 load balancer differ from an L7 one?
cards.a: L4 forwards by IP and port without reading the payload, so it is fast and protocol-agnostic. L7 terminates the connection and understands HTTP, so it can route by path or header at a higher CPU cost.

cards.q: Why does L4 balancing work poorly with long-lived HTTP/2 or gRPC connections?
cards.a: L4 balances per connection, but one connection can carry a huge number of requests, so load ends up skewed. An L7 balancer can spread individual requests across backends.

cards.q: When is least-connections better than round-robin?
cards.a: When request durations vary widely. Round-robin can keep feeding a server stuck with slow requests, while least-connections sends new work to the least busy one.

cards.q: How does NAT let many home devices share one public IP?
cards.a: The router rewrites each outgoing packet's source IP and port and records the mapping in a table. Replies to that public port are rewritten back to the private host.

cards.q: Why can an outside host not start a connection to a laptop behind NAT?
cards.a: No mapping exists until the inside host sends something, so the router does not know where to forward the packet. Port forwarding or hole punching works around this.

cards.q: Why can one server port handle thousands of clients at once?
cards.a: A TCP connection is identified by the 4-tuple of source IP, source port, destination IP and destination port. Clients differ in their source address or port, so they can all share the server's port.

cards.q: Which system calls set up a TCP server, in order?
cards.a: `socket`, `bind`, `listen`, then `accept` in a loop. `accept` returns a new socket for each client while the listening socket keeps waiting.

cards.q: Does a successful `send` mean the peer received the data?
cards.a: No. It only means the data was copied into the local kernel send buffer. Only an application-level reply can confirm the peer got it.

cards.q: Why does `epoll` scale better than `select`?
cards.a: `select` makes the kernel and the caller scan the whole descriptor set on every call. `epoll` keeps the interest set in the kernel and returns only ready descriptors, so cost follows activity rather than connection count.

cards.q: What happens between typing a URL and seeing the page?
cards.a: The browser resolves the hostname through DNS, opens a TCP connection and runs the TLS handshake. It sends an HTTP request, often answered through a load balancer or CDN. It then parses the HTML, fetches subresources and renders the page.

cards.q: What work can a browser skip when you reload a page moments later?
cards.a: It can reuse the cached DNS answer and the open connection, which skips the TCP and TLS handshakes. Resources come from cache, or are revalidated with a conditional request that returns `304`.

cards.q: What is the difference between `401` and `403`?
cards.a: `401` means you are not authenticated, so send valid credentials and try again. `403` means the server refuses the request, and logging in again will not help.

cards.q: What do `502` and `504` from a reverse proxy each tell you?
cards.a: `502` means the proxy got an invalid response from the upstream server, such as a dropped connection. `504` means the upstream did not answer in time.

cards.q: Why retry a `503` but not a `400`?
cards.a: A 5xx says the server failed, which may be temporary. A 4xx says the request itself is wrong, so the same retry gets the same failure, with exceptions such as `429`.

cards.q: How do session cookies and JWTs differ in where state lives?
cards.a: A session cookie holds a random ID and the server looks up the session in a store, which makes revocation easy. A JWT carries signed claims, so servers verify it without a lookup, but revoking it before expiry is hard.

cards.q: Can a client read the contents of a standard JWT?
cards.a: Yes. It is signed, not encrypted, and the payload is only base64url-encoded. The signature stops tampering but gives no secrecy, so secrets do not belong in it.

cards.q: What do the `HttpOnly`, `Secure` and `SameSite` cookie flags each protect against?
cards.a: `HttpOnly` hides the cookie from JavaScript, which limits theft through XSS. `Secure` sends it only over HTTPS, which stops network sniffing. `SameSite` limits sending it on cross-site requests, which reduces CSRF.

cards.q: Who enforces CORS, and what does it actually restrict?
cards.a: The browser enforces it. It stops a page's script from reading a response from another origin unless the server allows that through CORS headers. Tools such as `curl` and server-side code are unaffected.

cards.q: When does a browser send a preflight `OPTIONS` request?
cards.a: Before a cross-origin request that is not "simple", such as one using `PUT`, custom headers or a JSON content type. The real request goes out only if the server's `Access-Control-Allow-*` headers approve it.

cards.q: Why does CORS not stop CSRF?
cards.a: CORS limits reading the response, but a CSRF attack only needs the request to be sent with the victim's cookies. A plain cross-site form post goes out with no CORS check, so the defences are `SameSite` cookies and CSRF tokens.

cards.q: How does a WebSocket connection get established?
cards.a: The client sends an HTTP GET with an `Upgrade: websocket` header, and the server replies `101 Switching Protocols`. The same TCP connection then carries framed messages in both directions.

cards.q: Why are WebSockets harder to scale than plain HTTP?
cards.a: Each client holds a long-lived connection to one server, so servers carry many open sockets and rebalancing is hard. A message for a user on another server must be routed there, usually through pub/sub.

cards.q: What does it mean for an HTTP method to be idempotent, and which common method is not?
cards.a: Idempotent methods such as `GET`, `PUT` and `DELETE` leave the server in the same state however many times they repeat. `POST` is not idempotent, so a retry may repeat its effect.

cards.q: `DELETE` returns `200` and then `404` on a retry. Is it still idempotent?
cards.a: Yes. Idempotency is about server state, not the response, and the resource is gone either way.

cards.q: When should a client use `PUT` rather than `POST` to create a resource?
cards.a: When the client chooses the URL. Repeating `PUT /users/42` leaves one resource, while retrying `POST /users` lets the server pick a new ID each time and can create duplicates.

cards.q: Why was IPv6 needed?
cards.a: IPv4's 32-bit space of about 4.3 billion addresses ran out, which is why NAT became so common. IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses, so every device can have a global address.

cards.q: How does IPv6 handle fragmentation differently from IPv4?
cards.a: IPv6 routers never fragment packets. Only the sender can, and it relies on path MTU discovery, whereas IPv4 routers may fragment in transit unless the Don't Fragment bit is set.

cards.q: What does each letter of ACID protect against?
cards.a: Atomicity guards against half-applied transactions, consistency against broken constraints, isolation against interference from concurrent transactions, and durability against losing commits in a crash.

cards.q: How does the C in ACID differ from the C in CAP?
cards.a: ACID consistency means a transaction moves the database from one valid state to another, respecting constraints. CAP consistency means linearizability: every read sees the latest completed write across replicas.

cards.q: Which anomaly does each standard isolation level stop?
cards.a: Read committed stops dirty reads. Repeatable read also stops non-repeatable reads. Serializable also stops phantoms and behaves as if transactions ran one at a time.

cards.q: How does a non-repeatable read differ from a phantom read?
cards.a: In a non-repeatable read, re-reading the same row gives a different value. In a phantom read, re-running a range query returns a different set of rows because another transaction inserted or deleted matches.

cards.q: Two transactions read a counter, add one and write it back. What can go wrong under read committed, and how do you fix it?
cards.a: Both read the same value, so the second write overwrites the first and one update is lost. Use an atomic `SET x = x + 1` update, lock the row with `FOR UPDATE`, or add an optimistic version check.

cards.q: How can two doctors both go off call under snapshot isolation when a rule requires one to stay?
cards.a: Each transaction reads a snapshot showing the other still on call, then updates only its own row. The writes touch different rows, so no conflict is detected. This is write skew, and serializable isolation prevents it.

cards.q: How does MVCC stop readers and writers from blocking each other?
cards.a: A write creates a new row version instead of overwriting the old one. Readers use a snapshot and see the newest version committed before it, so neither side waits. Writers to the same row still conflict.

cards.q: Why does Postgres need `VACUUM`?
cards.a: Updates and deletes leave old row versions behind. `VACUUM` reclaims the ones no transaction can still see, otherwise tables and indexes bloat.

cards.q: Why can one long-running transaction slow down an MVCC database?
cards.a: Old row versions must be kept for as long as that transaction might read them, so cleanup cannot remove them. Tables bloat and other queries wade through dead versions.

cards.q: Why not put an index on every column?
cards.a: Every index must be updated on each insert, delete and relevant update, so writes get slower. Indexes also take disk and memory, and many would never be used.

cards.q: When is a hash index worse than a B+ tree index?
cards.a: Whenever a query needs order, such as range filters, prefix matches or `ORDER BY`. Hashing scatters keys, so it only serves exact equality.

cards.q: Why might the planner ignore an index and scan the whole table?
cards.a: If the filter matches a large share of rows, many random index lookups cost more than one sequential scan. The planner estimates this from table statistics.

cards.q: Why does `WHERE LOWER(email) = 'a@b.com'` skip a plain index on `email`?
cards.a: The index is ordered by raw `email` values, not by `LOWER(email)`, so it cannot seek on the result. Create an expression index or keep the column bare.

cards.q: How does a clustered index differ from a secondary index?
cards.a: A clustered index stores the rows themselves in key order, so a table can have only one. A secondary index stores the key plus a reference to the row, which in InnoDB is the primary key.

cards.q: Why can a random UUID primary key slow inserts in InnoDB?
cards.a: InnoDB clusters rows by primary key, so random keys land all over the tree, causing page splits and cache misses. Sequential keys append at the right edge instead.

cards.q: Why do databases use B+ trees rather than binary trees on disk?
cards.a: A B+ tree node fills a disk page and holds hundreds of keys, so the tree stays only a few levels deep. Each level can cost a disk read, and a binary tree would need dozens of levels.

cards.q: Why does a B+ tree keep values only in linked leaves?
cards.a: Keys-only internal nodes stay small, which raises fan-out and lowers height. Linked leaves let a range scan walk sideways without climbing back up the tree.

cards.q: How does an LSM tree absorb writes so quickly?
cards.a: A write goes to a log and an in-memory table. When that table fills, it is flushed as a sorted immutable file, and background compaction merges those files. Random writes become sequential disk I/O.

cards.q: Why are point reads usually slower in an LSM tree than in a B+ tree, and what helps?
cards.a: A key may sit in the memory table or in any of several sorted files, so a read may check many places. Bloom filters let it skip files that cannot contain the key.

cards.q: When would you pick an LSM tree over a B+ tree?
cards.a: For write-heavy workloads, since writes are batched and sequential. B+ trees suit read-heavy workloads and give steadier reads, because LSM compaction adds background load.

cards.q: Which filters can use a composite index on `(a, b, c)`?
cards.a: Filters on a leftmost prefix: `a`, `a, b` or `a, b, c`. A filter on `b` alone cannot seek, because the index is sorted by `a` first.

cards.q: Why do equality columns go before range columns in a composite index?
cards.a: Within one value of a column, entries are sorted by the next column. After a range condition, later columns are no longer sorted across the matched entries, so the index cannot seek on them.

cards.q: Why can a covering index make a query much faster?
cards.a: The index holds every column the query needs, so the database answers from the index alone and skips the random reads into the table.

cards.q: What do you look for first in the plan of a slow query?
cards.a: Full scans of large tables, and big gaps between estimated and actual row counts. Bad estimates usually mean stale statistics, which `ANALYZE` refreshes.

cards.q: What goes wrong if a customer's email is stored on every order row?
cards.a: An update anomaly: changing the email means updating many rows, and missing one leaves contradictory data. Normalisation stores each fact once.

cards.q: What does third normal form forbid?
cards.a: Non-key columns that depend on other non-key columns. If `zip` determines `city`, storing both in every row risks contradictions, so `city` moves to a table keyed by `zip`.

cards.q: When would you denormalise on purpose?
cards.a: When a read path is hot and joins are too slow, such as keeping a comment count on a post. The price is keeping the copies in sync on every write.

cards.q: When is each of nested loop, hash and merge join the best choice?
cards.a: Nested loop suits a small outer input with an index on the inner side. Hash join suits large unsorted inputs with an equality condition. Merge join suits inputs already sorted on the join key.

cards.q: Why can a `WHERE` condition on the right table turn a `LEFT JOIN` into an inner join?
cards.a: Unmatched rows have NULL in the right table's columns, and a condition such as `r.status = 'x'` filters them out. Move the condition into the `ON` clause to keep them.

cards.q: Why can `SUM(o.total)` come out too high after joining `orders` to `order_items`?
cards.a: Each order row repeats once per matching item, so its total is added several times. Aggregate the items in a subquery first, or sum at the item level.

cards.q: When does optimistic locking beat pessimistic locking?
cards.a: When conflicts are rare. It takes no lock and checks a version number at write time, retrying on conflict, whereas pessimistic locking makes every transaction wait. Under heavy contention the retries cost more than waiting.

cards.q: What does a database do when two transactions deadlock?
cards.a: It detects a cycle in the wait-for graph and aborts one transaction as the victim. The client must be ready to retry it.

cards.q: How does two-phase locking give serializability?
cards.a: A transaction acquires locks in a growing phase and releases them in a shrinking phase, never acquiring after a release. Any two conflicting transactions are then forced into one consistent order.

cards.q: Why should you avoid calling an external API inside a database transaction?
cards.a: Locks and a connection stay held for an unpredictable wait, which blocks others. If the commit then fails, the external effect cannot be rolled back.

cards.q: What is the core rule of write-ahead logging, and why does it matter?
cards.a: A change's log record must reach stable storage before the modified page does. After a crash, the log lets the database redo committed work and undo uncommitted work.

cards.q: Why is committing through a log faster than writing the changed data pages?
cards.a: A commit needs only a sequential append and a flush of the log, while data pages would need random writes across the disk. Dirty pages go to disk later in batches.

cards.q: What do you trade between synchronous and asynchronous replication?
cards.a: Synchronous replication waits for a replica, so failover loses no acknowledged write, but commits are slower and a stuck replica can stall them. Asynchronous replication commits fast, but a failover can lose the latest writes.

cards.q: A user saves a profile and sees the old one on refresh. What is the likely cause and fix?
cards.a: Replication lag: the read hit an asynchronous replica that has not applied the write yet. Route that user's reads to the primary for a while, or wait until the replica reaches the write's log position.

cards.q: Why does multi-leader replication need conflict resolution?
cards.a: Two leaders can accept different writes to the same row at the same time, and neither blocks the other. They must later reconcile with a rule such as last-write-wins or an application merge.

cards.q: Why do read replicas not increase write throughput?
cards.a: Every replica has to apply every write, so all writes still funnel through the primary. Scaling writes takes sharding.

cards.q: How do range sharding and hash sharding trade off?
cards.a: Range sharding keeps adjacent keys together, so range scans are cheap, but sequential keys pile onto one shard. Hash sharding spreads keys evenly, but a range query must touch every shard.

cards.q: Why choose a shard key that keeps common queries on one shard?
cards.a: Cross-shard queries fan out to many nodes and need merging, and cross-shard transactions need a protocol such as two-phase commit. Both add latency and failure modes.

cards.q: Why can two-phase commit block if the coordinator crashes?
cards.a: A participant that voted yes cannot decide alone, because others may have committed or aborted. It holds its locks until the coordinator recovers.

cards.q: What does the CAP theorem actually force you to choose?
cards.a: During a network partition, a system must either reject some requests to stay consistent or answer them and risk stale data. With no partition, there is no forced choice.

cards.q: What does PACELC add to CAP?
cards.a: It covers the normal case. With a partition you choose availability or consistency, and otherwise you choose latency or consistency, because synchronous replication takes time even when nothing is failing.

cards.q: Why does `hash(key) % N` break down when servers are added or removed?
cards.a: Changing N remaps almost every key, not only those on the changed server. For a cache, that means a sudden wave of misses.

cards.q: How does consistent hashing limit how many keys move?
cards.a: Servers and keys hash onto a ring, and each key belongs to the next server clockwise. Adding or removing a server moves only the keys in its arc, about 1/N of the total.

cards.q: Why does consistent hashing use virtual nodes?
cards.a: Each server takes many ring positions, which evens out load. A failed server's keys then spread across many servers rather than all landing on one neighbour.

cards.q: How do you choose between a relational database and a document store?
cards.a: Pick relational when you need joins, ad hoc queries and multi-row transactions. Pick a document store when records are self-contained, are read and written as a whole, and have varying schemas.

cards.q: What is the catch with a schemaless database?
cards.a: The schema moves into your application code. Every reader must handle every old document shape that still exists.

cards.q: What is the N+1 query problem, and how do you fix it?
cards.a: Code fetches a list and then runs one more query per item, often through lazy loading in an ORM. Fix it with a join or a single `WHERE id IN (...)` query, which ORMs call eager loading.

cards.q: How do `WHERE` and `HAVING` differ?
cards.a: `WHERE` filters rows before grouping and cannot use aggregates. `HAVING` filters groups after aggregation.

cards.q: Why does `WHERE x = NULL` return no rows?
cards.a: Any comparison with NULL yields unknown, not true, and `WHERE` keeps only true rows. Use `IS NULL`.

cards.q: How does `COUNT(*)` differ from `COUNT(col)`?
cards.a: `COUNT(*)` counts rows. `COUNT(col)` counts only rows where `col` is not NULL.

cards.q: Why can `x NOT IN (SELECT y FROM t)` return no rows at all?
cards.a: If any `y` is NULL, the comparison for a non-matching `x` becomes unknown rather than true, so no row passes. `NOT EXISTS` avoids this.

cards.q: In standard SQL, why can a `SELECT` alias not be used in `WHERE`, even though `ORDER BY` can use it?
cards.a: Clauses run logically as `FROM`, `WHERE`, `GROUP BY`, `HAVING`, `SELECT`, `ORDER BY`, `LIMIT`. `WHERE` runs before `SELECT`, so the alias does not exist yet.

cards.q: How do you turn 1 million requests a day into requests per second in your head?
cards.a: A day is about 86,400 seconds, so round it to 100,000. That gives roughly 10 requests per second on average, before any peak factor.

cards.q: Ten million users each upload 1 MB a day. What is the rough storage per year?
cards.a: That is 10 TB a day, so about 3.6 PB a year. Multiply by the replication factor for raw capacity.

cards.q: A service sends 1 MB responses at 1,000 requests per second. What bandwidth does it need?
cards.a: 1 GB per second, which is 8 Gbps. Remember to convert bytes to bits, because links are rated in bits.

cards.q: Roughly how long do a main memory read, an SSD read and a disk seek take?
cards.a: About 100 ns, 100 microseconds and 10 ms. Each step is 100 to 1,000 times slower than the last, which is why caching in memory pays off.

cards.q: Roughly how does a round trip inside a datacenter compare with one across an ocean?
cards.a: About 0.5 ms inside a datacenter and about 100 ms across an ocean. The long trip is limited by the speed of light in fibre, so faster servers do not help.

cards.q: Why does a page making 10 sequential cross-region calls feel slow however fast your servers are?
cards.a: Each call costs a round trip of around 100 ms, so the page spends about a second on the network alone. Batch the calls, run them in parallel, or move the data closer.

cards.q: How does cache-aside work, and what is its weakness?
cards.a: The app checks the cache, and on a miss it loads from the database and fills the cache. Writes go to the database and invalidate the key. The weakness is that a race or failed invalidation can leave stale data.

cards.q: How do write-through, write-back and write-around caching differ?
cards.a: Write-through writes to cache and database together, so writes are slower but consistent. Write-back writes to cache and flushes later, which is fast but risks loss. Write-around writes only to the database, so rarely read data never fills the cache.

cards.q: Why delete a cache key on write rather than update it?
cards.a: Two concurrent writers can update the cache in a different order from the database, which leaves a wrong value until it expires. Deleting makes the next read load the current value.

cards.q: How do LRU and LFU eviction differ in their failure modes?
cards.a: LRU evicts what was used longest ago, so it adapts quickly but one large scan can flush hot keys. LFU evicts what is used least often, so it protects steady hot keys but old favourites can linger after they go cold.

cards.q: How can one popular key expiring overload a database?
cards.a: Every request that misses goes to the database for the same value at once, which is a cache stampede. A per-key lock lets one request refresh while the others wait or use the stale value.

cards.q: Why add random jitter to cache TTLs?
cards.a: Keys loaded together, such as after a deploy, otherwise expire together and cause a wave of misses. Random offsets spread the expiry out.

cards.q: How do repeated requests for keys that do not exist get past a cache, and what stops them?
cards.a: With nothing to cache, every request reaches the database. Cache the negative result briefly, or check a Bloom filter of existing keys first.

cards.q: How does a token bucket allow bursts while capping the average rate?
cards.a: Tokens refill at a fixed rate up to the bucket's capacity, and each request spends one. A full bucket allows a burst up to its capacity, but the long-run rate cannot exceed the refill rate.

cards.q: How does a leaky bucket differ from a token bucket?
cards.a: A leaky bucket queues requests and drains them at a constant rate, which smooths traffic. A token bucket lets a saved-up burst through at once.

cards.q: What is the weakness of a fixed-window rate limiter?
cards.a: A client can spend its full quota at the end of one window and again at the start of the next. That allows twice the limit in a short span.

cards.q: What do sliding-log and sliding-counter rate limiters trade off?
cards.a: A sliding log stores a timestamp per request, which is exact but uses memory. A sliding counter weights the previous window's count by its overlap, which is cheap but approximate.

cards.q: How do you enforce one rate limit across many servers?
cards.a: Keep the counters in a shared store such as Redis and update them atomically, so every server sees the same count. The cost is a network hop per request.

cards.q: What do you gain by putting a queue between two services?
cards.a: The producer does not wait for the consumer, the consumer can be slow or down for a while, and bursts are absorbed. The cost is added latency and more moving parts.

cards.q: How does a log-based broker such as Kafka differ from a traditional work queue?
cards.a: A work queue removes a message once a worker acknowledges it. A log keeps messages for a retention period and each consumer group tracks its own offset, so consumers can replay and read independently.

cards.q: Where does Kafka guarantee ordering?
cards.a: Only within a partition. Giving related messages the same key sends them to the same partition, which gives per-key ordering.

cards.q: Why does a queue consumer need a dead-letter queue?
cards.a: A poison message that always fails would otherwise be retried forever, wasting work or blocking the queue. After a set number of attempts it is moved aside for inspection.

cards.q: What decides whether a consumer gets at-most-once or at-least-once delivery?
cards.a: When it acknowledges. Acknowledge before processing and a crash loses the message. Acknowledge after processing and a crash causes redelivery, so duplicates are possible.

cards.q: Why is exactly-once delivery not achievable over an unreliable network, and what is used instead?
cards.a: If an acknowledgement is lost, the sender cannot tell whether the message was processed, so it must risk a loss or a duplicate. Systems use at-least-once delivery with idempotent processing to get an exactly-once effect.

cards.q: How does an idempotency key stop a retry from charging a card twice?
cards.a: The client sends the same unique key with each attempt at one operation. The server stores the key with the result, so a repeat returns the saved result instead of charging again.

cards.q: How do you make a message consumer safe against duplicates?
cards.a: Record each processed message ID in the same transaction as the side effect, or write with an upsert keyed on a natural ID. A redelivered message then changes nothing.

cards.q: How does requiring a majority vote prevent split brain?
cards.a: Split brain is two nodes both acting as leader after a partition. Any two majorities of a group overlap, so at most one side of a partition can elect a leader.

cards.q: Why is a lease not enough to guarantee a single leader, and what fixes it?
cards.a: A leader can pause, for example in a long GC, wake after its lease expired, and keep writing. Each lease comes with an increasing fencing token, and storage rejects writes with an older token.

cards.q: Why does R + W > N give reads that see the latest write?
cards.a: Any set of R replicas must overlap any set of W replicas in at least one node. The read therefore reaches a copy of the latest write, and version numbers identify it.

cards.q: Why do consensus groups use an odd size such as 3 or 5?
cards.a: A majority of 5 is 3, so it survives 2 failures. A group of 6 needs 4, so it also survives only 2 and costs more.

cards.q: How does Raft elect a leader?
cards.a: A follower that stops hearing heartbeats waits a randomised timeout, then becomes a candidate in a new term and requests votes. Each node votes once per term, and a majority wins. The random timeouts make split votes rare.

cards.q: When is a Raft log entry committed?
cards.a: When the leader has stored an entry from its current term on a majority of servers. A future leader needs votes from a majority, and voters reject candidates with older logs, so it must hold that entry.

cards.q: How does a stale Raft leader find out it has been replaced?
cards.a: Every message carries a term number. When it sees a term higher than its own, it steps down to follower.

cards.q: How does linearizability differ from eventual consistency?
cards.a: Under linearizability, each operation appears to happen at a single instant, so reads always see the latest completed write. Under eventual consistency, replicas converge if writes stop, but reads may be stale until then.

cards.q: What do read-your-writes and monotonic reads each promise?
cards.a: Read-your-writes means a user always sees their own updates. Monotonic reads means a user never sees data go backwards by hitting a staler replica on a later read.

cards.q: Why is last-write-wins by wall-clock timestamp risky?
cards.a: Clocks on different machines drift, so a later write can carry an earlier timestamp. That write is then silently discarded.

cards.q: Why is cursor pagination better than offset pagination for deep pages?
cards.a: `OFFSET` makes the database read and discard every skipped row, and inserts shift pages so items repeat or vanish. A cursor such as `WHERE id > last_id LIMIT n` seeks through an index, so cost stays flat. You lose the ability to jump to page N.

cards.q: How do fan-out on write and fan-out on read differ for a news feed?
cards.a: Fan-out on write pushes each post into every follower's feed at post time, so reads are fast but writes are heavy. Fan-out on read assembles the feed at read time, so writes are cheap but reads are slow.

cards.q: How do you handle a user with 100 million followers in a fan-out on write feed?
cards.a: Skip the push for such accounts. Most posts are fanned out on write, and celebrity posts are merged in at read time.

cards.q: Why keep images in object storage rather than in the database?
cards.a: Large blobs bloat the database, its backups and its buffer cache. Object storage is cheap, durable and scales well, so the database keeps only metadata and the object key.

cards.q: Why let clients upload through a pre-signed URL?
cards.a: The client sends bytes straight to object storage, so app servers do not carry the upload traffic. The URL is short-lived and scoped to one object, so no storage credentials are exposed.

cards.q: Why does a search engine use an inverted index instead of scanning documents?
cards.a: It maps each term to the list of documents containing it. A query reads only the lists for its terms and intersects them, so cost follows the matches rather than the corpus size.

cards.q: Why does a search index usually lag behind the primary database?
cards.a: It is a derived copy, updated asynchronously from a change stream or queue, so recent writes take time to appear. In exchange, it can be rebuilt from the source at any time.

cards.q: What are the four golden signals of monitoring?
cards.a: Latency, traffic, errors and saturation.

cards.q: Why watch p99 latency rather than the average?
cards.a: An average hides a slow tail. A page that fans out to many backends hits some backend's tail on most requests, so the tail is what users feel.

cards.q: Why should latency of failed requests be tracked separately from successful ones?
cards.a: Fast failures pull the numbers down, so a service returning instant errors can look healthy. Mixed together, the figure describes neither case.

cards.q: Why shed load during overload instead of queuing every request?
cards.a: Queued requests can time out before they are served, so the server wastes work on replies nobody reads. Rejecting some early keeps the rest fast.

cards.q: Why does a stalled reader of a TCP stream eventually block the writer?
cards.a: The reader's receive buffer fills and its advertised window drops to zero. The sender's buffer then fills and `write` blocks, which is backpressure built into the protocol.

cards.q: A service handles 100 requests per second at 200 ms each. How many are in flight on average?
cards.a: 20, by Little's Law: items in the system equal arrival rate times time in the system. It also shows that slower responses mean more concurrent requests.

cards.q: Why does latency shoot up as utilisation nears 100 percent?
cards.a: Arrivals are bursty, and with little spare capacity each burst queues behind the last. Waiting time grows non-linearly, so latency explodes before the server is fully busy.

cards.q: What does a circuit breaker do, and why?
cards.a: After too many failures it opens and fails calls immediately instead of waiting on a sick dependency. That frees the caller's threads and gives the dependency room to recover.

cards.q: What is the half-open state of a circuit breaker for?
cards.a: After a cool-down, the breaker lets a few trial requests through. Success closes it and failure opens it again, so it recovers without flooding the dependency.

cards.q: Why must every remote call have a timeout?
cards.a: Without one, a stuck dependency ties up the caller's threads or connections until the caller stalls too. One slow service then spreads into a cascading failure.

cards.q: Why add jitter to exponential backoff?
cards.a: Clients that failed together would otherwise retry together, hitting the recovering service in synchronised waves. Random delays spread the load over time.

cards.q: How can retries make an outage worse?
cards.a: Each layer's retries multiply load on a service that is already struggling. Three layers that each try three times turn one request into 27 attempts at the bottom.
